# GridTwin ZA - verified results

Findings fit to quote externally, each with the scenario that produced it. A
number without its scenario is not a result. Every entry states the weather year
and the period, because an annual figure and a July figure are not comparable.

THE SCENARIO INCLUDES THE PANEL'S OWN CONTROLS, not just the external comparison.
Added 15 Sep 2026 after three entries in one day could not be reproduced from what
was written down: the retail headlines, which do not record basis, scenario year,
or whether the figure is a week or an annual mean; the battery saturation table,
which did not record the reserve price; and the derived knee, which recorded a
number the code no longer produces. Every entry must carry the preset, the
scenario year, and every toggle that is not at its default. An entry that cannot
be re-derived from what it states is not a result either.

SECOND CAVEAT, 2 Oct 2026: every adequacy figure below for a build that KEEPS COAL predates the
engine charging storage from coal ahead of stress, and is pessimistic by some amount. Directions
re-measured on three key entries all hold; levels do not. See "Which earlier findings the charging
fix touches".

Third caveat, 8 Oct 2026: every result from the build optimiser (the national build LP, bldBuildLP, and the
regional one, bldBuildRegionalLP) on a build before `2026-10-08c` is provisional. Both LPs kept one storage energy
balance per day, so a store could discharge in the morning energy it charged that afternoon (entry "Why the engine
sheds where the optimiser served in full"). Build `2026-10-08c` gives the national LP an hourly state of charge (entry
"Hourly state of charge in the build LP"); the regional LP still has the daily balance (TODO 14bn),
and no regional optimiser result is to be published until it is fixed with 14bj (user, 8 Oct). Entries whose main
finding is an optimiser output carry "pending the storage fix" in the heading and stay as written until re-run.
Engine-only results (dispatch, adequacy checks of a fixed build, preset searches scored on the engine) are unaffected.

WEATHER YEARS (corrected 14 Oct 2026, user; this caveat used to say all of it was one synthetic-normal year).
One year of hourly shapes, the default profile set (profiles.json): the app's single runs, every preset figure, and the
suite's findings, invariants, consistency, response and outputs checks; the build optimiser's representative days also come
from it. Twelve weather years (2014-2025, with outage draws): the pathway engine check (pathcheck.js) behind every c-run's
adequacy verdict and engine PV, the build loop's per-year adequacy test and the stress windows it adds, the weather and
benchmark checks that say so, and the MTSAO external check. Entries before 8 Oct 2026 mostly rest on the one year; each
entry's own settings say which. A bad wind year is what sets a capacity requirement, so one-year results are the ones
to read as optimistic.

## The system cost was missing a third of itself

Build `2026-09-20a`, 18-19 Sep 2026. Two costs that no system-cost aggregate had ever carried
were added in one session. `avgCost` at defaults went R548.06 to R883.50/MWh.

**Fixed O&M for the existing fleet, R61.6bn/yr, 34% of system cost at defaults.** Before this,
`totalCost` and `gridCost` were fuel plus carbon plus new-build capital. Medupi cost fuel and
carbon; Koeberg cost essentially nothing. Staff, maintenance, overhauls, insurance and rates
were absent for 39.7 GW of coal and everything else already built.

THE BIAS RAN ONE WAY. Retiring coal appeared to save only fuel and carbon when it also stops a
maintenance bill that does not fall with output. Every coal-versus-renewables comparison this
model has produced understated the case for replacement. Retiring 27 GW now saves R31.4bn of
O&M the model previously could not see.

Calibrated to Eskom's own filing, not to benchmarks: Generation MYPD 6 (NERSA, Aug 2024)
Table 1 gives R55,093m of opex over the Table 4 fleet of 46,686 MW. Our constants reproduce
that to 99.9% on that fleet. Relative weights across technologies are international
(European vintage study) because the filing gives no split.

  THREE CAVEATS. It is an APPLICATION, not an outturn, and NERSA applies a prudency test, so
  it is an upper bound. It includes CENTRALISED SERVICES allocated to Generation. And the
  per-technology split is the weakest part - Table 54 of the same filing would replace it.

**The REIPPPP PPA obligation, R11.7bn/yr.** Existing wind and solar cost the system NOTHING
before this: there is no `costWind` or `costPv`, so their fuel and carbon are zero, and
`newCapexR` covers new build only. Nearly 8 GW of IPP renewables generated free electricity in
every scenario the model had ever run.

Only REIPPPP is charged - 4,042 MW wind and 2,783 MW solar. `by_source` separates the fleet to
the megawatt, and private wheeled (470/488) and Eskom-owned (100/0) carry fixed O&M like every
other existing asset. The distinction is not sunk cost: a PPA is a CONTRACT, not an asset, and
Eskom pays because it signed.

CHARGED ON DELIVERED OUTPUT. Curtailment up to 10% is uncompensated per the March 2024
Addendum and deemed energy above that is already modelled, so charging contracted output would
count the curtailed portion twice. Rolls off 2034-2041 as the twenty-year PPAs expire.

### Sunk capital stays out, and that is deliberate

PyPSA's convention: for existing plant the annuity is a constant in the objective and cannot be
avoided by any decision, while fixed O&M is exactly what `coalDecomMW` stops paying. Same
reasoning excludes stranded assets from system cost - retiring Medupi early consumes no
additional resources, it means capital is not recovered from customers. That is a transfer and
it belongs in the retail panel, which has a stranded basis.

## New-build capex was blind to ten years of learning

Build `2026-09-20a`, 19 Sep 2026. `newCapexR` read the flat `acap*` constants, which hold the
same quantity as `BLD_COST` + `BLD_FOM` and never decline. Rule 6: no constant appears twice.

Now derived from `bldCapex` at the scenario vintage. The same fossil-free build:

```
build year   newCapex R bn   totalCost R bn   avgCost R/MWh
2026                 520.7            537.5          2,609
2035                 462.6            478.4          2,309
2040                 434.5            445.7          2,143
2050                 386.1            396.4          1,893
```

GOING EARLY COSTS R49.3bn A YEAR, about 12%, between 2040 and 2050. BEFORE THIS FIX THE MODEL
SAID R1.2bn, all of it residual PPA. An answer to a live policy question was an artefact of a
duplicated constant.

Decline rates were already sourced - BNEF 2035: solar -30%, storage -25%, onshore wind -23%,
CCGT rising on the 16% jump BNEF recorded in 2025. Offshore's 2.6% comes from ESMAP instead, so
the table mixes sources.

VINTAGE IS THE MIDPOINT and that is correct, not a simplification. A 2040 scenario is a fleet
built progressively from 2026, so its average capex is the midpoint; pricing it all at 2040
would assume nothing was built until the final year. Assumes a LINEAR build-out - a real
transition is back-loaded, so this is mildly conservative.

## Offshore wind is not near baseload

Build `2026-09-20a`, 18 Sep 2026. Twelve weather years, Renewables.ninja / MERRA-2 at seven
ESMAP regions, levels scaled to ESMAP Tables 16 and 17, shapes as measured.

```
group        CF      hours below 10% of rating   longest drought   CV
offshore     0.516                       18.2%              83 h   0.69
onshore      0.368                       14.1%              35 h   0.67
```

The ESMAP report describes offshore as having lower variability and providing near baseload
capacity. ON THESE PROFILES IT DOES NOT. Offshore delivers 40% more energy and spends MORE of
the year effectively absent. Droughts run 62 to 103 hours against 22 to 45 onshore. Every
offshore region has a first-percentile hour of exactly zero; every onshore region has a
positive floor.

AND SIX OF SEVEN REGIONS TROUGH IN MAY, the seventh in June, while onshore troughs spread
across February and March. Seven sites over 2,000 km of coastline and three weather systems,
all failing in the same month. Whatever spatial diversity offshore buys, it does not buy
SEASONAL diversity - and seasonal is what the winter wind drought is about.

### The siting objection, tested and dismissed

The first measurement compared developer-selected onshore sites (capacity-weighted centroids of
real REIPPPP plants) against arbitrary offshore water, which is not a fair test. Three
candidates per region were screened on 2018 and the best kept. Result: 18.3% -> 18.2%, drought
79 h -> 83 h. NOT A SITING ARTEFACT.

The turbine cuts the same way and strengthens it: a V164 8000 has LOWER specific power than the
onshore V90 2000, so it should be flatter. It is not.

CAVEAT: MERRA-2 is reanalysis at about 50 km and will understate short sharp lulls at every
site, so absolute drought lengths are soft. The comparison between them is not.

## Headroom is where the wind is not

Build `2026-09-20a`, 19 Sep 2026. `headroom_summary.json` against `regional_renewable_capacity`:

```
region            headroom MW   existing wind   existing solar   wind CF
Northern Cape               0             790           1,283      0.379
Eastern Cape                0           1,896               0      0.367
Western Cape                0           1,257             359      0.365
Hydra Central               0             669             460      0.425
KwaZulu-Natal           5,500               0               0      0.216
Gauteng                 4,680               0              50      0.247
Limpopo                 3,360               0             506      0.235
Mpumalanga              3,320               0               0      0.255
North West              1,660               0             445      0.332
Free State              1,420               0             169      0.268
```

EVERY REGION HOLDING EXISTING WIND HAS ZERO HEADROOM. All 19,940 MW of it sits in regions with
almost no renewables and the worst resource in the country.

That is the South African grid problem in one table, and it is why a national average cannot
represent congestion: a national figure divides capacity in the Cape by headroom in Gauteng.
A scaled national derate was built on 19 Sep and REMOVED the same day for exactly this reason -
it looked more authoritative than a flat 4% while resting on no better foundation.

The 4% itself is NERSA's Congestion Curtailment Framework CEILING, the most an IPP may be
curtailed before compensation, used as though it were an expected rate.

## A fossil-free system fails a stability constraint the model was not checking

Build `2026-09-20a`, 19 Sep 2026. `SYNC_MIN_MW` is 6,000 MW and only coal, nuclear, hydro and
imports counted toward it. Non-coal synchronous plant is 3,460 MW, so the balance came from
coal via `Math.min(cAvail, syncDeficit)`.

WITH NO COAL THAT TERM IS ZERO AND THE FLOOR WAS SILENTLY UNMET. The fossil-free build ran at
3,460 MW against a 6,000 MW requirement in every hour and reported nothing.

Grid-forming batteries and synchronous condensers now count:

```
Fossil-free 2040, 30% grid-forming        floor met in all 8,760 hours
Fossil-free, 0% grid-forming              floor UNMET in all 8,760 hours
Fossil-free + 2 GW synchronous condensers floor met
```

SO A FOSSIL-FREE SOUTH AFRICA IS FEASIBLE ON SYSTEM STRENGTH ONLY IF ABOUT 30% OF THE STORAGE
FLEET IS GRID-FORMING - 12 GW at this build. If none of it is, the system fails every hour
regardless of how much energy it has.

### Do not add synchronous condensers

AEMO is moving AWAY from them: a July 2026 report has them turning to battery inverters because
syncons are proving expensive and hard to find. South Australia, past 50% renewables, installed
four totalling about 508 MVA for AUD 166m, with 1,670 MVA more identified - and the pivot to
inverters came before the next tranche was built.

AEMO ALSO SAYS INERTIA IS NOT THE PROBLEM. Declaring shortfalls under an 80%-renewables-by-2030
scenario they foresaw no issues on inertia; what binds is SYSTEM STRENGTH, the fault level at a
node, in MVA. Our single national MW floor stands in for both, which is the same category of
error as a national congestion derate.

UPDATED 23 Sep 2026, AEMO's FY26 Engineering Roadmap webinar. Frequency, inertia and voltage
control are now business as usual there, where inertia was the headline challenge a few years
ago, and AEMO has opened a three-part workplan on whether grid-forming batteries can substitute
for synchronous machines in meeting minimum system strength. The reason is ours: syncons have
become expensive and slow to deliver while the grid-forming battery fleet has grown.

BUT THE SUBSTITUTION IS NOT SETTLED. AEMO's 2025 position was that protection-quality fault
current remains a key limitation of grid-forming inverters, and its own simulations and early
hardware-in-the-loop relay testing find that misoperation of some protection elements is
possible. Trials with market participants and an ARENA-funded UNSW project run through 2026,
with the Transition Plan for System Security due in December.

WHAT THIS MODEL CANNOT SEE, stated rather than modelled. The binding property is protection-
quality fault current at a node, in MVA, and it depends on the control strategy of the inverters
installed - responses are software, and they vary by manufacturer, where a synchronous machine's
is physics and predictable. A national megawatt floor cannot represent that, and SYNC_GFM_SHARE
0.30 is a bracket for a substitution ratio that the one market testing it has not yet fixed.

### Inertia is worth R4.6bn a year to storage, and it was invisible

Pricing reserve and inertia in Fossil-free 2040:

```
reserve revenue   R0.24bn/yr
inertia revenue   R4.59bn/yr        totalCost unchanged at R445.7bn in all cases
```

Nineteen times the reserve revenue, essentially all of it to the battery fleet. Both were
recorded as pure TRANSFERS - system cost does not move. That was verified on Fossil-free 2040
only, where unserved energy is zero either way, and it does not generalise. See the correction
below. Both toggles now default ON in the two high-renewables presets: leaving
inertia unpriced in a 2040 system models a market that cannot exist. They stay OFF for Today
2026 and Crisis 2023, where South Africa genuinely prices nothing.


### Correction, 21 Sep 2026: reserve is now held whether priced or not

Build `2026-09-21c`, 21 Sep 2026. Presets as stored, default weather year and worst of twelve.

Operating reserve is a flat 2,200 MW (`reserveOperatingMW`, NTCSA ASTR 2026/27-2030/31 Table 7),
held every hour priced or not. Dispatch may not take spare capacity below it; demand beyond that
is shed. Storage counts only as far as it can sustain output for one hour (`asHoldHours`).
Pricing now changes payments only: unserved energy is identical priced and unpriced.

```
unserved GWh                   build 21b     build 21b     build 21c
                              pricing off    pricing on
Today 2026         default           2.7           2.7          50.4
                   worst of 12        23            23           205
Deep decarb 2035   default          83.6          85.3         112.9
                   worst of 12       203           196           268
Fossil-free 2040   default             0             0             0
                   worst of 12         0             0             0
Crisis 2023        default        17,281        17,281        29,817
```

Fossil-free 2040 stays at zero in all twelve years. Today 2026 reaches Stage 4 in the default
year, against Stage 2 before; mean wholesale price R1,101 to R1,440/MWh.

Caveat: Today 2026 has not been checked against Eskom's 2025 load-shedding record. Do not quote
it until it has.

Caveat: totalCost carries no cost of unserved energy, so Crisis 2023 falls from R363.6bn to
R282.1bn while shedding 12.5 TWh more. Do not compare system cost across runs that shed
different amounts.

Reserve and inertia pricing are now pure transfers: unserved energy, totalCost and avgCost are
identical priced and unpriced on Today 2026, Deep decarbonisation 2035 and Fossil-free 2040.
The R445.7bn figure above predates the 18-20 Sep cost basis; Fossil-free 2040 reads R453.6bn.

`validate_invariants` asserts on six cases that pricing leaves unserved energy unchanged, and
that unserved energy rises with the requirement.

### Demand re-anchored to 2026, exports counted once, 21-22 Sep 2026

Build `2026-09-22a`. Generator `build_demand_2026.py`, reading ESK19679 directly.

RSA Contracted Demand includes exports (it equals Residual Demand plus Total RE, a supply-side
measure), and the engine adds its own firm exports, so 6.6 TWh was counted twice. The series is
now contracted demand less exports: calendar 2025 hourly shape, scaled by 0.9442, the Jan-Aug
2026 vs Jan-Aug 2025 ratio of domestic demand. Domestic grid demand 194.6 -> 183.8 TWh.

The 0.938 ratio used on 21 Sep came from a harness note and was not reproducible: contracted
demand including exports falls by 0.920, domestic demand by 0.944. Exports fell 9.7 -> 5.7 TWh.

```
                       unserved GWh default      worst of 12       avgCost R/MWh
                       21c      21d     22a      21c   21d   22a     21c    22a
Today 2026             50.4     3.5     0         205    40   5.4     880    901
Deep decarb 2035      112.9    41.0     0         268    80  11.5   1,549  1,785
Fossil-free 2040          0       0     0           0     0     0   2,184  2,563
```

### ORDC read the requirement as availability, 22 Sep 2026

Build `2026-09-22f`. `marketPriceSeries` compared the engine's reserve requirement, read as if it
were reserve available, against 6% of peak through `asReserveFrac`, a key that does not exist.
The engine now returns `reserveAvailMW` per hour (committed coal headroom within its ramp, storage
discharge headroom sustainable for one hour, and charging that can stop), and the ORDC compares it
with the hourly requirement. The only callers are the retail panel's market basis: the annual
shadow rows (`retailRaw`) and the week chart (`retailHourly`).

```
                        scarcity hours      market R/kWh     engine R/kWh
```

in Crisis 2023) while Eskom's ILS was 0.07 TWh: its industrial curtailment sits inside MLR.

Correction: RSA Contracted Demand already includes load shed. Residual demand counts MLR, ILS and
IOS as resources (2023: 208.7 TWh of generation plus 16.8 TWh of reductions = 225.9 contracted).
The Crisis 2023 demand set on 22 Sep added the shed load a second time. Fixed: 214.6 TWh domestic,
+16% on the 2026 base (was +24%).

```
Crisis 2023, +24%               26.7                    16.75
Crisis 2023, +16%               13.8
```

in place of the modelled outage path.

```
                         model outages   actual availability   actual
2025 conditions, GWh          277               270              570
Crisis 2023, TWh             14.3              10.7            16.75
```

With actual availability, 2025 shedding moves into January to May, as it happened; the modelled
path spread it across the year because it has no within-year fleet improvement. The level stays

(Koeberg 11.5 TWh against 8.1 in 2023 and 10.2 in 2025; wind, solar and RMIPPPP hybrids about 6
TWh above 2023), and wheeled private plant is probably counted twice, once as supply and once
by its absence from contracted demand (about 2.5 TWh a year). Unverified.

The preset spills half its wind and solar potential: it was sized for higher demand and for

midday. Leaner builds cut R0.5-0.9/kWh.

Why this differs from Australia's outlook: AEMC's falling prices come from renewables displacing
wholesale prices of A$100/MWh and more. South Africa's baseline is depreciated coal at about
R0.58/kWh of fuel and carbon. Unspilled new wind costs about R0.75/kWh (37% capacity factor) and
solar R0.64 (24%) at this model's 2030 capex and 8%; that is roughly cost-neutral, but at 50% spill it doubles.

Open, not changed:
- The residential allocation (1.622, Eskom cost-to-serve C12 against the system) multiplies the
  whole stack, so every generation cost increase is scaled by 62%. Residential's premium is
  mostly network and retail. Needs the cost-to-serve study's component split.
- Price per grid kWh is not the bill: 20 GW of new rooftop cuts grid sales and raises fixed cost
  per kWh while rooftop households' bills fall. AEMC reports bills as well.
- New transmission at R6,964 per kW of all new wind and solar is the TDP average; solar sited
  near load needs less.

Storage dispatch against perfect foresight (ldes_series.js, ldes_lp.js at the repo root).
Fossil-free, weather year 2020 (its worst), 16.8 GW new rooftop. The surplus and deficit are taken
from an engine run with no new storage; the LP then dispatches the new storage optimally against
them, cyclic over the year, efficiencies as the engine's (lithium 0.88, iron-air 0.45).

```
new storage                        engine shed GWh   perfect-foresight shed GWh
45 GW lithium 8h                         25.8                   0.0
35 GW lithium 8h                            -                  58.1
25 GW lithium 8h                            -                 138.1
35 GW lithium + 2 GW iron-air            64.6                   0.0
```

The engine's rule-based dispatch leaves 26 GWh unserved that optimal dispatch avoids, and it
handles iron-air badly: 2 GW of 100-hour storage discharged 27 GWh in the engine and took 58 GWh
of shortfall to zero in the LP. The finding that iron-air never helps is a finding about the
dispatch rule, not the technology. Perfect foresight is an upper bound: real operators forecast
days, not a year. The LP also ignores reserve holding, which the engine does.

Transmission overlap. The regional reinforcement charge prices capacity beyond existing plus
TDP-built headroom; the flat R402/kW-yr prices every new MW at the TDP average. Capacity beyond
headroom pays both:

```

Deep decarbonisation 2035        64.8 GW       5.2 GW      R1.22bn         R2.08bn
Fossil-free 2040                 83.4 GW      11.6 GW      R2.67bn         R4.65bn
```

The two charges also count different capacity: reinforcement includes the solar on retired-coal
sites, which the flat charge exempts.

### Long-duration dispatch fixed; both presets re-optimised with iron-air, 22 Sep 2026

Build `2026-09-22ae`.

The fix. In a deficit hour, if lithium alone is projected to run short within 48 hours, stores
of 100 hours or more discharge first at up to their power, keeping lithium for the peak hours.
The projection is net load before storage less firm thermal capacity. Otherwise lithium still
goes first. Found by testing rules against the perfect-foresight LP on Fossil-free 2020: pure
lithium-first leaves a low-power 100-hour store unable to cover the peaks once lithium is empty;
long-first cycles iron-air daily at 45% and wastes it.

```
Fossil-free, weather year 2020        before   after   perfect foresight
35 GW lithium + 2 GW iron-air         64.6      5.1           0
25 GW lithium + 3 GW iron-air        105.6     10.4           0
45 GW lithium only                    25.8     25.8           0
```

The lithium-only gap is not this rule. 29.7 GWh of that run's residual is operating reserve
held on storage and passed to peakers that a fossil-free system does not have, which the LP
ignores; with reserve holding off the engine still sheds 21.4 GWh in four hours against a greedy
0 on the same residual. Open: in those four hours demand response returns 1,200 MW of shifted
load into the shortage.

Re-optimised, twelve weather years, NEM standard:

```

35 W / 35 S / 35 GW Li                              306.6           2.7      19.6
35 W / 35 S / 25 GW Li + 1 GW iron-air (preset)     298.6           2.4      18.0 (2016)
35 W / 35 S / 20 GW Li + 2 GW iron-air              299.2           0.5       5.0
35 W / 35 S / 20 GW Li + 1 GW iron-air              289.5           4.8      misses

Fossil-free 2040 (limit 3.46 GWh)
10 off / 30 W / 55 S / 45 GW Li                     359.5           2.2      25.8
10 off / 30 W / 55 S / 30 GW Li + 2 GW iron-air     352.2           2.4      26.4
 7 off / 35 W / 55 S / 35 GW Li + 2 GW iron-air     350.2           2.5      30.2 (2020) preset
 5 off / 40 W / 55 S / 35 GW Li + 2 GW iron-air     348.2           3.9      misses
```

Iron-air now earns its place: R8.0bn a year off Deep decarbonisation and R9.3bn off Fossil-free.
Supersedes the finding that iron-air appears in no robust build; that was the dispatch rule.

### The NTCSA MTSAO mismatch: professional practice and what the 86 GWh assumes, 22 Sep 2026

Build `2026-09-22af`, no code change.

How professional adequacy models dispatch storage:

```
AEMO ESOO        storage fully optimised to reduce unserved energy, perfect foresight;
                 AEMO notes the risk is greatest for very short storage and penalises
                 2-hour batteries for it
ENTSO-E ERAA     sequential Monte Carlo (Antares, among others), perfect foresight one week
                 ahead; a share of capacity is reserved for balancing and not dispatched
NTCSA MTSAO      Monte Carlo on demand, wind, solar and unplanned outages, "dispatching
                 available generators optimally", multi-nodal, results the mean of samples
```

All three dispatch storage to minimise shortfall with foresight longer than 48 hours. The
adequacy hold is in line with practice and more conservative than it; selling ahead of coal
regardless of a coming shortfall was the outlier.

What the 86 GWh is (MTSAO 2026-2030, section 7.4.1.2): high EAF (67%), moderate demand
(264 TWh in 2030, Mozal assumed to 2030), all new capacity with the 6 GW of CCGT delayed,
8.4 GW of coal and Cahora Bassa's 1.15 GW gone by March 2030, reserves of 3,800 MW held,
Monte Carlo mean, transmission-constrained.

The engine on the harness scenario, with and without the hold:

```
                                          with hold   without
default weather, one outage path             4.4        54.1
20 outage draws, mean                        4.6        39.6
12 weather years x 3 draws, mean            13.0        37.9
same, 3.8 GW less utility solar             22.9           -
```

The old agreement came from dispatch that sold storage ahead of coal, which none of the
professional models do. What the engine still lacks against the MTSAO:
- Monte Carlo averaging in the check: the mean over weather years and outage draws is three
  times the single run.
- Transmission: the MTSAO is multi-nodal and attributes part of its unserved energy to
  network constraints; the engine is national.
- The capacity mapping: the MTSAO's all-new category is 29.7 GW in 2030 including the 6 GW
  of gas, so about 23.7 GW without it, rooftop included. The harness enters 27.5 GW. Not
  confirmed; the category breakdown is in figures that do not extract as text.

(wind 4,400, PV 10,900, rooftop 1,800, batteries 2,150 MW, against 6,700 / 15,000 / 3,800 /
2,000 entered before); coal EAF 64, the project's conversion of the MTSAO's 67% fleet EAF;
0.34 GW of Acacia and Port Rex retired.

```

rebuilt, coal EAF 64 (the check)            211.7       86     55    fails, +125.7
rebuilt, coal EAF 67                         76.1       86     55    passes
old inputs, 36-draw mean                     13.0       86
```

The EAF conversion decides the check. The engine sheds with peakers at full output and coal at
its available ceiling, so the shortfall is real in the model. Still missing: the MTSAO's
transmission component, which would raise its figure relative to a national model, not lower it.

### Where the NTCSA gap comes from, 22 Sep 2026

Build `2026-09-22ag`, no code change. Rebuilt MTSAO case, mean of twelve weather years x two
outage draws, against NTCSA's 86 GWh:

```
                                                    mean shed GWh
rebuilt check as it stands                              240.7
+ Cahora Bassa at 1,150 MW all year                      79.9
+ non-Eskom firm plant, 2,100 MW                         43.3
+ both                                                   12.1
+ non-Eskom firm and Cahora Bassa pro-rata (288 MW)      32.0
+ the same at coal EAF 67 instead of 64                   9.1
```

Two inputs, not the EAF conversion, carry most of it:

- Cahora Bassa. The check zeroes imports for all of 2030; the MTSAO has the contract running to
  March 2030. A quarter of it, 288 MW on an annual average, is worth 55 GWh of shed energy here.
- Non-Eskom plant. The MTSAO counts 2,387 MW of non-Eskom generation contributing 10.5 TWh -
  1,328 MW coal, 582 gas, 198 cogeneration, 180 pumped storage. The model's fleet is Eskom's
  only, so that capacity is absent from every scenario, not just this check.

The old check read 13 GWh because its 8 GW of surplus new renewables offset the missing firm
capacity. Two errors cancelling.

Open question before the check is fixed: whether the demand series covers the load those
non-Eskom plants serve. Eskom contracted demand is 210.5 TWh in this case against the MTSAO's
264 TWh national figure, and the difference is losses, exports, rooftop self-consumption and
possibly that load. Adding their generation without their demand would flatter the model.

than the inputs are known: 5% more demand took the same case from 186 to 635 GWh, and a flat
availability derate in place of the unit-level outage model took it from 186 to 43.

```
unserved energy                   4.5 TWh            more than 4 TWh
OCGT utilisation                   47.6%             about 45%
```

Not measured: the 72-hour mean repair time. ESK19679 carries fleet capability loss, not per-unit

### Outage repair time sourced and calibrated, 22 Sep 2026

Build `2026-09-22ai`. The 72-hour mean repair time was unsourced. Two routes were tried.

Published figures do not fit this fleet. Deakin et al. (2022), comparing outage models against
ENTSO-E data, use 40 hours for coal with 0.86 availability, after Edwards et al. (2017). The same
paper finds those Markov models far less persistent than the real data they represent: European
fleets show a week-lag autocorrelation of 0.27 to 0.70 against about zero in the model.

So the value is calibrated to persistence instead, from Eskom's own hourly series. Unplanned
capability loss in 2025 has an autocorrelation of 0.91 at a day, 0.70 at a week and 0.44 at a
month; total fleet availability, 0.92 and 0.79. The modelled availability path against those:

```
repair time h      24 h lag    1 week lag
 40                  0.54         0.21
 72 (was)            0.77         0.29
120                  0.84         0.34
240                  0.88         0.47
480 (now)            0.96         0.74
observed                0.92         0.79
```

It changes little: a 2025 backcast goes 4 to 7 GWh of shed energy, the NTCSA risk-adjusted case
4.8 to 4.5 TWh. What matters is unit-level outages at all, not their length - the same case reads
43 GWh with a flat availability derate against 186 with unit-level outages. Both presets still
meet the reliability standard: Deep decarbonisation 3.35 GWh mean shed against its 3.67 limit,
Fossil-free 3.09 against 3.46.

Two checks were reading one outage draw and now average three, because at 480 hours a single path
carries several GWh of noise: the reserve-requirement invariant (7.7 / 5.0 / 227.3 GWh on the base
seed, which inverts the first two) and the 2026 surplus benchmark (8.6 GW on the base seed, 6.5 as
a three-draw mean).

### The 2025 backcast, and what it says

Bigger than the repair time: at 2025 conditions the model sheds 4 to 7 GWh where Eskom shed
390 GWh (the same figure the MTSAO reports for the year to September). Demand is not the reason -
the model's 196.1 TWh and 29.6 GW peak match contracted demand ex-exports of 194.7 TWh and 30.5 GW.
Nor is diesel: the model burns 0.26 TWh against Eskom's 3.4 TWh of OCGT, so Eskom shed load while
burning more fuel than the model uses.

What is left is the shape of availability. Real 2025 fleet availability has a fifth percentile of
54.5% and a minimum of 46.7% around a 62.4% mean, and those troughs persist for weeks. The
modelled path has a similar spread but disperses faster. The fix that professional models use is
to drive the simulation with historical availability traces rather than synthetic draws - MISO
builds hourly outage adders from GADS history, AEMO uses historical reference years. ESK19679
carries the hourly series to do it.

### Historical availability traces built; the backcast gap is not availability, 22 Sep 2026

Build `2026-09-22aj`. `nodal/coal_availability_trace.json` holds measured coal-only availability
for 2023, 2024 and 2025 from ESK19679: Eskom installed capacity less planned, unplanned and other
capability loss, less nuclear at its measured output and the other 5,758 MW at 90%, over coal
capacity. Each year is divided by its own mean, so the file carries shape and the level stays
the scenario's coalEAFPct. Set outageTraceYear and coal availability follows that year's measured
hours instead of the Markov draw; unset, nothing changes. A check asserts both the level and the
persistence.

Correction to the entry above: that 2025 backcast ran the 2026 fleet against 2025 availability -
wind 4,512 MW rather than about 3,900, solar 3,271 against 2,600, rooftop 8,942 against 6,900,
batteries 800 against 500, Medupi 4 and Kusile 6 already back. On the 2025 fleet it sheds 13 GWh
rather than 7.

The trace does not close the gap. On the 2025 fleet and the measured 2025 shape the model sheds
1.6 GWh, against 13 for the Markov draw and Eskom's actual 390 GWh of load shedding.

What the Eskom data says about those hours. Load was reduced in 1,048 hours of 2025, and in them
demand averaged 26.2 GW while coal generated 20.0 GW - against roughly 23 GW of coal that was
nominally available at that year's availability. Eskom reduced load with about 3 GW of available
coal not generating, and burned 3.4 TWh of OCGT doing it, against this model's 0.6 TWh. So the
binding difference is not how much plant is available but how much of it can actually be
delivered in the hour: minimum stable levels, ramp limits, units available but not synchronised,
and reserve protection. The model treats available capacity as dispatchable up to its commitment
schedule.

The trace is worth having regardless - it is the right input for backcasts and removes a
synthetic assumption from them - but the calibration item stays open and now has a direction.

### The 2025 backcast decomposed; a Backcast 2025 preset, 22 Sep 2026

Build `2026-09-22ak`. Eskom shed 390 GWh in 2025 and burned 3.4 TWh of OCGT doing it. The 202
hours in which it shed, against the model driven by the same measured availability:

```
                        Eskom actual   model
demand                     24,645        23,634   (Eskom includes 1,566 MW of exports)
coal available             19,588        19,865
coal generated             18,943        17,975   (the model holds 2,200 MW of reserve)
OCGT                          942           655
pumped storage                390           423
load shed                   1,931             8
```

Deliverability is not the problem: Eskom's coal generated 96.5% of its available capacity in
those hours and 98.5% in the year's 200 highest-demand hours, so there is no systematic 3 GW of
available-but-undeliverable plant. The earlier reading of that came from comparing those hours
against the annual mean availability rather than the hour's own.

Three inputs explain most of the rest, and two were again 2026 values on a 2025 run:

- Exports. FIXED.exportsMW is 745 MW, the post-Mozal level. Exports averaged 1,705 MW in 2025
  and 1,566 in the hours Eskom shed. Correcting it takes the backcast from 2 to 6 GWh.
- Peakers. The model dispatches the full 3.06 GW OCGT fleet when short; Eskom managed 942 MW in
  those hours while using 3.4 TWh over the year. Limiting the fleet to what Eskom delivered takes
  the backcast to 131 GWh.
- The rest is demand: the model's year is 204.5 TWh against contracted 209.6.

```
2025 backcast, cumulative              shed GWh
as first run (2026 fleet)                    7
2025 fleet                                  13
+ measured availability trace                2
+ 2025 export level                          6
+ peakers held to 1.4 GW                   131
Eskom actual                               390
```

New preset, Backcast 2025: the 2025 fleet, demand, exports and measured coal availability in one
place, so this cannot be run on today's fleet by accident again. It sheds 6 GWh.

Open: why Eskom's peakers delivered under a gigawatt in its tightest hours while the model
delivers three. Fuel logistics and station availability are the candidates, and neither is in
ESK19679.

### Common-mode trips added; Today 2026 expected shedding roughly triples, 3 Oct 2026

Build `2026-10-03d`. Professional tools (GE MARS, AEMO's ESOO, PLEXOS) draw forced outages unit by
unit, independently; correlation is added as a common-mode failure rate that takes a group out
together, with its own repair rate (Billinton and Allan; Singh). Done here per station, with the
independent rate reduced so the EAF is unchanged. 0 events reproduces the independent draw exactly.

Calibrated to ESK19679 2023-2025 on two statistics, checked on two it was not fitted to:

```
                            measured            calibrated (60 draws)
days losing >8% in 24h      9, 16, 16           14       fitted
largest 6-hour fall         0.136-0.152         0.154    fitted
1st percentile              0.73-0.83           0.78     not fitted
worst week                  0.76-0.87           0.80     not fitted
```

5 events per station-year, each taking half the station's units, 36-hour repair (February 2025:
8 of 10 tripped units back within about a day and a half).

Today 2026, 960 draws, each with its own outage path and one of twelve weather years:

```
                         mean shed GWh   worst-year mean
independent                  0.07              0.7
common-mode                  0.19              2.0
null, same random use        0.06              0.7
```

At 48% EAF, eight draws: 0.102 to 0.111 TWh. Still under the 0.002% standard (about 4 GWh) at
today's fleet. Coal presets other than Today 2026 not yet re-measured over many draws.

### A coal operating floor does not reproduce 2025's curtailment either, 4 Oct 2026

Build `2026-10-04a`, Backcast 2025, stopgap off (curtailment setting 0). Test only, in a copy: coal
held at or above a share of its available capacity in every hour.

```
floor      night coal mean / p5 / min    curtailment         at night (22-05)
none         18,355 / 15,667 / 14,054    0
55-70%       unchanged                   0
80%          18,186 / 15,194 / 12,994    5 GWh, 0.03%        100%
85%          18,061 / 15,340 / 13,224    697 GWh, 3.9%       42%
90%          18,376 / 16,046 / 14,002    3,214 GWh, 18%      33%
Eskom 2025   19,177 / 16,144 / 13,210    about 1.0-1.6%      mostly night
```

The floor does not bind until about 80% of available coal, then curtailment jumps past the target
in one step and lands mostly at midday on solar, not at night on wind. Wrong timing and no stable
setting in between. Together with the minimum-stable test (up to 1.4x, no curtailment) and the
demand-definition test (ruled out), no system-wide mechanism tried reproduces 2025: night
curtailment of about 1% with clean days.

The remaining explanation is local: NERSA says plants were curtailed to keep the grid stable at
low demand, which on long, lightly loaded lines in the Northern and Eastern Cape points to voltage
or stability limits at specific substations, not national surplus. A single-node dispatch cannot
produce that. The stopgap stays; its timing could be moved to wind at night.

On the grid basis the engine dispatches (after rooftop, before exports), 2026 series, profiles.json against the open
candidate (open_final.json): peak 28.80 against 28.95 GW; load factor 73.4% against 73.1%; hours above 27 GW 113
against 48; mean of the top 100 hours 27.83 against 27.12 GW, top 500 26.35 against 25.90 GW; June-August 17:00-20:00
mean 25.76 against 25.18 GW. The entry above compared peaks and load factors with rooftop added back (30.6 against
28.9 GW, 75% against 79%); on that basis profiles.json peaks at 10:00 in July, which the engine never dispatches, so
that comparison overstated the difference in the peak and understated it in the hours near the peak.

Finding: the demand shape is a first-order input for adequacy. At the same annual energy and almost the same single
peak, the open shape's thinner tail of near-peak hours halves the shed, so taking it unadjusted would understate
adequacy needs. Matching annual energy and the single peak (two constants) would not close the gap, since the peaks
already match. Decision (user, 12 Oct): keep the current profiles for c4 and its seeded set; afterwards test the open
shape quantile-mapped to the measured load-duration curve (a small set of derived constants) and propose the public
swap only if it reproduces c3's shed within about 10%. Eskom data credited (Eskom Holdings SOC Ltd, ESK19679); the
statistics are GridTwin ZA's analysis, not Eskom's; no hourly series is reproduced. Caveats: one build (c3); ESRG's
hourly year is a modelled year; the shape-only case serves 1.2% more energy (rooftop add-back on its own solar shape).

read-only hook that records each hour (no engine change; scratchpad sn_run.js). Today 2026 preset, default profiles, outageSeed

availability; nuclear 1,240.8, hydro 331.1 and imports 1,012 MW must-take; coal available each hour as the engine had it (its
reserve withholding included, which is none this week: fast-start 6,924 MW against a 2,200-2,343 MW need); the 84 UC_FLEET units
standing in 2026, scaled to 39,692 MW (39,692/41,530, as the engine's commitment pre-pass), with their minimum stable levels

Energy pairs are engine / PyPSA unit commitment. Lithium cycles: discharge over 129,339 MWh.

Why: the engine discharges storage only in each day's top quartile of hours or against a forecast shortfall (simulate(),
index.html ~7665 and the charge targets after it), so lithium sits near full: in the May week it holds 53-129 GWh at 06:00 each day
and 23 of 31 curtailed hours begin with lithium at least 90% full; PyPSA empties it overnight and refills it from the
midday surplus. Coal and gas fall by what the extra 0.4-0.5 TWh of lithium discharge displaces.

For 14dl (user): the engine charges coal start-ups twice, once per unit start in the UC pre-pass and once per MW of the main
loop's aggregate commitment rising. In 2040 the second charge is R11.0-14.6m a week, 0.3-1.0% of the week's engine cost; at
that rate about R0.6-0.8bn a year against c4's R372.6bn in 2040 (rough scale, three weeks only).

24-hour rolling optimum (user, 13 Oct 15:00; scripts validation/single_node/sn_pypsa40_roll.py on branch claude/sn-crosscheck):
the same model and inputs, but each day is optimised seeing that day and the next 24 hours (a 48-hour window, the last one 48
hours to the week's end); the first 24 hours are kept and the window moves on a day, carrying each unit's status and hours in
it, each store's state of charge and the coal ramp. A store's energy left at a window's end has no value to the optimiser, so a
rule is needed: 'fe' holds iron-air (100 hours) at least at its level at the window's start; 'all' does that for every store.
The last window keeps the engine's end-of-week levels. HiGHS, mip_rel_gap 0.1%, every window optimal.

Finding (user, 13 Oct): with 24 hours of sight PyPSA lands within 0.0-1.0% of the full-week optimum (rule 'all') or 1.1-7.1%
('fe'), and the engine stays 30-48% above it, so the gap is the engine's storage rule, not foresight. In the stress week PyPSA
sheds nothing, with the full week's sight and with 24 hours, against the engine's 37.3 GWh on the same build (c4 with its 1,000
MW top-up), the same weather and the same outage draw. So the engine check's 2040 shortfalls, and the top-ups sized to them,
are partly the engine's storage scheduling rule (which discharges only in each day's top-quarter hours or against a forecast
shortfall), not only a lack of capacity. One week of one draw; the share of the 2040 top-up this explains is not measured.

Operating share, for sizing (user, 13 Oct; c4's engine check, the 480-run local re-run of 13 Oct, scratchpad engsplit): fuel
(variable O&M and the pre-pass start-ups included), carbon, the per-MW start-ups and shed are R826.8bn of c4's R2,597.7bn PV

(27.8%). If the three weeks' gap against the rolling optimum (23-33% of the engine's operating cost) held across 2040, c4's
2040 engine cost would be overstated by R24-34bn (6-9%); earlier years carry less storage (2026 baseline week 2.2%), so the
2026-40 overstatement is smaller than 31.8% x 23-33%; not measured.

Caveats: three weeks, not a year; one outage draw each. Single node, as the engine. Three weeks, not a year. Both sides use the engine's

### Like-for-like cross-check on c5b_14r's weeks (engine build 2026-10-14r): with reserve, Avon and Dedisa must-run and interruptible load on the PyPSA side, the engine is 1.1-3.5% above the 24-hour optimum on the 2026 baseline, 2040 May and 2040 November, but 26.0% above on the 2040 stress week and 3.1-26.0% (median 8.6%) on c5b_14r's 15 worst stress weeks; the engine sheds 123.0 GWh across those 15 weeks and the optimum none, with the additions on or off (user, 15 Oct 2026, message 116)

Finding. Mark (1) of TODO 14dt (within 5%) passes on the three ordinary weeks and fails on the 2040 stress week and on 13 of the 15
stress weeks with all three additions on (12 of 15 with them off). Mark (2) (no more shed than the optimum) fails on all 15. The
15 were chosen as the engine's worst shedding weeks, so the engine shedding in all of them is by construction; the finding is that
the optimum sheds in none of them under any setting. The 14dx (2) reading of the remaining shortfalls (the engine holds coal as
reserve that the optimum does not) does not hold on 14r: with the same reserve products on the PyPSA side, the optimum covers
them in every hour of every week (shortfall 0.00 GWh, against the engine's 1.35-70.87 GWh a week) and still sheds nothing. In
the three largest stress weeks and the 2040 stress week the optimum discharges 1.4-2.1 times the engine's lithium energy, runs
more CCGT and less diesel. The must-run accounts for the 2026 baseline: 5.6% with it off, 1.2% with it on (14d: 1.2%). The
reserve products add nothing measurable to the optimum's cost: in a single 168-hour window, reserve on and off differ by 0.2 R m
or less, within the 0.1% MIP gap.

Caveat. Between settings, the rolling optimum moves by up to 1.0% for reasons of the rolling windows, not the settings (an added
constraint lowered the rolling cost on May, November and stress; the single-window solves show it does not lower the full-week
cost). Read differences between settings below about 1% as noise. Both sides see the week's actual load, weather and outages
(48 hours for the optimum, the engine's look-aheads as in 'Known limitation: the engine's look-aheads read the actual future').
One bus, one outage draw per week. Provisional in the same sense as the c5b_14r sensitivities: for the reviewer.

### Wind diagnostics on c5b_14r (engine and optimiser build 2026-10-14r; nothing changed): the optimiser's 12 calendar days give new wind a 33.9% capacity factor against 45.2% over the twelve weather years, and tracking solar 33.1% against 28.7%, so on the optimiser's own days new wind costs R1,094/MWh against solar's R714 in 2030, where over the twelve years the two are level (R821 and R823); s_windlow builds 23.6 GW of wind to 2040 against c5b_14r's 17.0 GW (user, 15 Oct 2026, message 117)

Finding. The build optimiser (bldBuildLP) prices energy on 12 calendar days of the default profile year, each weighted 365/12
(bldRepDays(12): the tightest net-load hour, the slackest day, the middle of the worst 3-day net load, the middle of the worst
3-day wind lull, and evenly spaced days), plus stress windows that carry their own weather year's shapes at small weight. On those
12 days new wind (modern-turbine profile x 1.064) runs at 33.9% and tracking solar at 33.1%. The same profiles average 44.3% and
34.2% over the default year, and 45.2% (41.8-47.8%) and 28.7% (27.4-29.6%) over the twelve weather years the engine check
uses. So the optimiser sees new wind about a quarter weaker and tracking solar about a seventh stronger than the engine does.
The default profile's own fixed-tilt solar is 25.1% against 21.7-23.0% in every one of the twelve years (mean 22.4%), which
is where solar's half of the gap comes from; for wind the gap is the choice of days (the default year's own new-wind mean is
44.3%). This favours solar over wind in every c-run, by an amount not measured here.

Caveat. Capacity factor is not the whole of value: the 12 days carry the adequacy-relevant hours on purpose, and the stress
windows add the worst weeks. Whether the optimiser would build more wind on representative days that match the twelve-year
energy is not tested (no new runs). The capacity factors above are per unit of the profiles the engine and optimiser use;
BW6's preferred solar bids state 30.1% for tracking (IPP Office, 7 Nov 2025).

scripts and README there), run on each year's state as the engine check builds it, draw 0
(seed 71830529 + weather year x 7919), years 2030, 2035, 2040, GRID=1; the LP's cost terms are read from the app's own

over wind plus solar output plus vreCurtailed, mean of the twelve years. R/MWh: total R/kW-yr over (capacity factor x 8.76).

BW5 awarded tariffs (DMRE 28 Oct 2021, fully indexed, price base not stated): wind R495.22/MWh weighted (R344.25-617.70), about R631 (R438-787) in 2026 rands on SOURCES' approximate x1.273; solar R428.79 (R374.79-484.60), about R546.

Notes on (2). Fixed O&M is BW6's (R367 wind, R269 solar per kW-yr, January 2024 rands, x 1.068). The spur is the grid-cost option
(GRID=1): for bid capex that includes connection, only the distance beyond the 18 km median (22.0 km for wind, 9.7 km for solar),
on a 132 kV circuit at the ITP rate, over 40 years. Wind on the Cape allowance (cw) pays neither spur nor integration charge.
IRP 2025's fixed O&M, capacity factors, life and discount rate for wind and solar are in the gazette's Figure 9 ('New Technology
Cost Assumptions'), not read here (long PDF); the assumptions workbook gives capex only. The workbook says IRP 2025's wind and
solar starting costs are BW6's, as ours are; ours decline faster (wind 2.86% a year against the workbook's base case, which
reaches R22,598 in 2040 against our R18,960). BW5 tariffs are 20-year fully indexed prices, comparable in kind with a real
levelised cost, but at the bidders' own cost of capital and resource; the conversion to 2026 rands is approximate (SOURCES
'REIPPPP onshore wind tariffs'). On that basis c5b_14r's new wind in 2030 (R821/MWh over the twelve years, R720 without the
integration charge) sits about 14-30% above BW5's weighted wind tariff (about R631), and its tracking solar (R823, R663
without) above BW5's solar (about R546). BW6 awarded no wind; the BW6 bids are the capex basis here.

(3) Do the BW6 wind capex and the R402/kW-yr integration charge cover the same network? On the sources found, no, in principle;
the overlap risk sits elsewhere.
- BW6 capex: the IPP Office note (7 Nov 2025) does not define what the overnight cost includes. Under REIPPPP the IPP pays the
  shallow connection, to the nearest substation, and not the deep connection costs of strengthening the transmission system
  (Eberhard and Naude, Journal of Energy in Southern Africa 27(4), 2016, read). Bidders price it from Eskom's cost estimate letter.
  So BW6 capex most likely includes the dedicated connection and excludes upstream strengthening (connIncl in the code).
- R402/kW-yr: our derivation from TDP 2024's generation-integration spend (SOURCES 'Sources used for constants': R225bn for
  46.9 GW, R4,800/kW, 40 years at 8%). TDP 2024 Public Report Rev1 (December 2024), Table 4, FY25-29: capacity expansion R80.7bn,
  of which new generation integration R54.3bn and network strengthening R26.4bn, total R112.5bn (search extract). Rev2 (February
  2025): upstream works for IPPs are committed only once IPPs are preferred bidders (extract). NERSA's Transmission Tariff Code:
  'The connection charge is based on the cost of assets used for the benefit of a single customer' (extract). So generation
  integration is shared upstream network, recovered through use-of-system charges, not the IPP's dedicated assets.
- Where overlap can occur in the model: the spur charge. Bid capex already carries a typical connection, so the LP charges only
  the distance beyond the median; a project farther out than its bid assumed is charged twice for the excess only.
- The R402 itself (message 120 (1)): it rests on RESULTS 'Transmission reconciled to what the TDP buys' (22 Sep 2026, build
  2026-09-22ad), from TDP 2024 Rev 2, Table 4: new generation integration R54.3bn plus land and rights pro rata to capacity
  expansion (R4.9bn x 54.3/80.7), 51.2% of the five-year R112.5bn; that share applied to the decade's R440bn (DBSA; NTCSA
  CEO, August 2026) gives R225bn for 46.9 GW (56 GW less 9 GW of rooftop; 15.9 GW of it gas), R4,803/kW, and at
  8% over 40 years (annuity factor 0.0839) R403/kW-yr from these rounded figures, against the code's R402 (the 22 Sep entry's
  51.1%): a rounding difference, no change. The research helper's 48% (R54.3bn of R112.5bn) leaves out
  the land share; the two agree. Two assumptions are ours: the five-year share applied to ten years, and land pro rata. Not
  re-read from the primary document today: www.ntcsa.co.za is not reachable from this session and the report is too long for
  the fallback reader; the page number, Rev 1's figures and the GW the spend serves stay to be read from the PDF (pending).
- Flag on the rules: NERSA's wheeling network charge rules (Government Gazette 52781, 2025) let connection charges 'contribute to
  the upfront cost of the connection ... including any network strengthening' (extract); if applied to new IPPs, part of the deep
  cost would move into the generator's capex and the R402 would then double-count it.

Not used, unverified (message 120 (2)): Meridian Economics, 'Comparative analysis of IRP 2023 cost assumptions', 2 February
2024 (42 pages; the research helper read pages 1-12 only, with Firecrawl, against the rule for long PDFs). Figures drawn from
those pages, none used in any table above or in the reviewer pack, each unverified until the full document is read: IRP 2023's
wind capacity factor from CSIR/Fraunhofer profiles, 38.1% spatially averaged; EPRI's wind capacity factor 36.3%; IRP 2023's solar
capacity factor not specified; EPRI's solar 26.5% (CdTe) and 29% (crystalline silicon); CSIR/Fraunhofer fixed-tilt solar 19.6%
(16.8-22.6% by region); IRP 2023's wind and solar fixed O&M 'significantly higher' than other sources; IRP 2023's solar LCOE about
double the average BW6 successful bid price.

(4) Reduced cost of new wind in 2030, 2035 and 2040 from c5b_14r's own solution: not done. The run saves each solve's column

### PROVISIONAL: representative days test (s_repdays_c5b14r). With the optimiser's eight evenly spaced calendar days re-chosen so new wind and tracking solar match their twelve-year means, the optimiser builds 64% more wind by 2040 (27.9 GW against 17.0 GW) and 35% less utility solar (24.0 GW against 36.9 GW); engine PV 2026-40 falls R10.6bn (0.4%) and CO2 2026-40 falls 169.5 Mt (8.5%); every year passes the adequacy standard (engine build 2026-10-14r; user, 15 Oct 2026, message 122 (1)); test only, no model change

How the current days are chosen: bldRepDays(12) takes four days selected from the default profile (the tightest net-load hour, day 162; the slackest day, 195; the middle of the worst three-day net load, 218; the middle of the worst three-day wind lull, 359) and eight evenly spaced days (0, 45, 90, 135, 180, 225, 270, 315), each weighted 365/12, plus the weather-year tail days and stress windows. On those twelve days new wind runs at 33.9% against 45.2% over the twelve weather years, and tracking solar at 33.1% against 28.7% (TODO 14el).

### The engine sheds in c5b_14r's worst stress week because it never charges storage from gas and cycles pumped storage daily; the 24-hour optimum runs CCGT through the solar hours, banks 40-56 GWh in pumped storage and enters the last day with 40 GWh in its stores (engine build 2026-10-14r; user, 15 Oct 2026, messages 122 (2) and 123 (3)); no engine change

Week s01 of 'Like-for-like cross-check on c5b_14r's weeks' (2037, weather year 2021, hours 897-1064, seed 87939557): the engine
sheds 42.9 GWh, all in the week's last nine hours (hours 159-167 of the week), where both its stores are empty; the optimum (all
three additions on) sheds none. Hour by hour the two sides have the same coal availability (the same outage draw), the same coal
output in the shed hours (at availability, 9,352 MW), CCGT and diesel at their limits (5,886 and 3,709 MW), imports at 1,066 MW
and no reserve held on coal; the difference is the energy in storage when the last day starts:

| Hour of week | Load MW | Lithium stored, engine / optimum, MWh | Pumped storage stored, engine / optimum | CCGT and open-cycle LNG, engine / optimum, MW | Diesel, engine / optimum |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | 26,876 | 29,395 / 41,822 | 21,704 / 15,595 | 0 / 5,213 | 0 / 0 |
| 30 | 26,481 | 14,976 / 36,213 | 21,095 / 12,586 | 0 / 5,213 | 0 / 0 |
| 54 | 27,117 | 43,415 / 42,101 | 22,088 / 17,474 | 0 / 5,213 | 0 / 0 |
| 78 | 32,993 | 58,208 / 55,352 | 26,901 / 38,911 | 37 / 5,886 | 0 / 0 |
| 102 | 32,472 | 58,164 / 34,618 | 9,832 / 40,042 | 396 / 5,886 | 0 / 0 |
| 126 | 29,120 | 58,186 / 51,823 | 20,583 / 56,136 | 220 / 5,886 | 0 / 0 |
| 150 | 31,454 | 21,040 / 37,717 | 11,026 / 36,095 | 5,886 / 5,886 | 0 / 0 |
| 159 | 27,139 | 0 / 22,413 | 0 / 17,504 | 5,886 / 5,886 | 3,709 / 3,709 |

With only iron-air held at window ends (NEUTRAL=fe), the optimum enters hour 159 with 21,522 MWh of lithium and 18,395 MWh of pumped storage and sheds nothing.

Cause, from the hours above and the code (index.html at 6045387):
- The engine never charges storage from gas. With the storage look-ahead on (storageLookaheadH 48, every c5b_14r run), short
  stores charge from surplus and coal only ('They charge from coal only up to _laReq(h, 0)'), and the older gas-ahead-of-storage
  rule (_gasFirst) is switched off when the look-ahead is on (!_laOn). In solar hours the engine turns CCGT down to 0-400 MW;
  the optimum keeps it at 5.2-5.9 GW and puts the difference into storage.
- Pumped storage is cycled daily: the engine fills it to about 20 GWh by day and empties it most evenings (its hold rule,
  _laPsHold, sizes the hold on the 48-hour window). The optimum builds it to 39-56 GWh by days 3-5 and holds it.
- Not foresight: both sides see 48 hours. Not the optimum's end-of-window rule: with only iron-air held at window ends the
  optimum still enters hour 159 with 40 GWh in its stores. Not coal commitment, ramps, reserve, imports or outage draws: identical.

Fix options (no change before the user decides; effects are expected, not measured):
(a) let the look-ahead charge short stores from spare CCGT and LNG open-cycle plant when the window's need beyond coal exceeds what
    surplus will bring, as the optimum does. Expected to remove most stress-week shedding, since in all 15 stress weeks the optimum
    sheds none; fuel cost rises a little in those weeks, diesel and shed fall.
(b) pumped storage on the same look-ahead as lithium, with its own duration (60 GWh at 2,724 MW, 22 hours), so it banks over days.
(c) a longer look-ahead, 72 or 96 hours: helps only together with (a); measured cost about 15% more simulate() time per extra
    24 hours (engine fix (B), 14 Oct).
(d) for weeks that shed, an hourly optimum in place of the rule (as the cross-check does): closest to the optimum, heaviest.
Effect on the stress margin: c5b_14r needed a 3,000 MW stress margin for the engine check to pass; that margin covers the engine's
dispatch shortfall as much as capacity. With (a) and (b) the engine's stress-week shedding should move towards the optimum's zero,
so the margin needed, the top-ups and engine PV would all fall; by how much needs a re-run of the loop on the changed engine.

Settings: validation/single_node (PR #51) with an hourly dump added to sn_pypsa40_roll_x.py (DUMP_HOURLY, read-only: the
objective is unchanged, R4,118.9m); NEUTRAL=all and NEUTRAL=fe; X_RES=X_MR=X_IL=1.

### New wind's capacity factor (45.2%) against BW6 wind bids' own (37.24%), and new wind and solar cost against BW5 and BW7 tariffs on the same capacity factor basis: the model's 2026 cost is 41-49% above the tariffs before any grid charge (build 2026-10-14r; user, 15 Oct 2026, message 123 (1)-(2)); no change

(1) Capacity factor. The capex and fixed O&M of new wind come from BW6's compliant wind bids, whose 'typical capacity factor' is
37.24% (IPP Office REIPPPP historical data note, 7 Nov 2025; definition not stated). New wind in the model runs at 45.2% over the
twelve weather years. The gap, step by step:
- Profile and turbine: Renewables.ninja MERRA-2 output for a Vestas V162 5.6 MW at 120 m hub height at the 98 sites of
  profile_sites.json, mapped onto each weather year (build_wind_modern.py), uncorrected: 42.5% (45.2 / 1.064).
- The 1.064 correction (+2.7 points): fitted to two farms' annual output as projected by their developers, not measured (message
  124 (2)): Impofu (Enel Green Power, 330 MW, '1,260 GWh annually', 43.6%; Enel's project page, an annual estimate; the cluster reached
  full commercial operation in May-June 2026, Engineering News, 30 Jun and 2 Jul 2026) and San Kraal (EDF, 140 MW, 616 GWh, 50.2%;
  commercial operation 11 Dec 2025, Engineering News, 11 Dec 2025; the 616 GWh figure's source was not found again on 15 Oct 2026 and
  is unverified). Neither farm had a full year of metered output when the correction was fitted (7 Oct 2026), so the correction rests on
  two projections, over four weather years (check_wind_farms.py). Both are new, large-rotor farms at strong sites.
- Site mix: the 98 sites carry the model's national weighting; BW6's wind bids were all in the Eastern and Western Cape supply
  areas (gov.za, 8 Dec 2022). Per-bid capacity factors are not published, so the site effect cannot be separated.
- Other benchmarks: the existing fleet's profile 37.0% (reanalysis corrected to metered output by 0.848); the REIPPPP wind fleet
  produced 11,040 GWh in 2025 on 3,763 MW at year end, about 33% (our division of Engineering News, 9 Jan 2026, and SolarQuarter,
  10 Apr 2026, search extracts; the fleet grew during the year); IRP 2023's CSIR/Fraunhofer 38.1% and EPRI 36.3% (Meridian,
  unverified, see 'Wind diagnostics on c5b_14r').
Judgement: 45.2% is defensible only for the best new sites and largest rotors; for a programme of 17-24 GW over 2026-40 it is the
top of the range, and the bids that set its cost assumed 37.24%. Defensible central range on the evidence found: about 38-43%.
The 'low' correction (1.00) gives 42.5%. A capacity factor on BW6's basis would also need BW6's capex, which is the pair used here.

(2) Cost per MWh against tariffs, 2026 rands, same capacity factor basis (2026 capex; 8% real over 25 years; fixed O&M as in the
model). Tariffs are 20-year, fully CPI-indexed prices (BW5: 'weighted average Fully Indexed Price'; BW7: indexation not stated in
the sources found, assumed fully indexed), so comparable in kind with a real levelised cost, at the bidders' own cost of capital.

solar entry. Caveats: price bases are not published (April 2021 and January 2024 assumed); BW5 was bid before the 2022 turbine

The consistency check 'CCS lowers emissions when enabled' (validate_consistency) failed at the new default: 133.88 against 157.51

threshold only a near-full share reaches. At 21.8% the expected coal emission factor is (1 - 0.9 x 0.218) / (1 - 0.25 x 0.218) =
0.850 of unabated, and the run gives 133.88 / 157.51 = 0.850, so capture is applied as intended. Fixed (user, message 157 (3)): the
check keeps its 0.5 threshold and pins ccsSharePct 100 in its run, 22.39 against 157.51 Mt, pass. A new check, 'CCS at the default
share cuts emissions part of the way', requires the run at FIXED.ccsSharePct to fall between the two: 133.88 Mt, pass.

### New gas pays its full annualised capex, fixed O&M and LNG terminal charge whatever it runs; no published price or revenue figure is labelled energy-only (user, 16 Oct 2026, message 130 resent; TODO 14an); report only, no model change

Gas. Build 2026-10-16b (the gas cost terms are unchanged from 16a). The engine's capital line (newCapexR in simulate) charges
every new MW of gas the annuity of its capex at the vintage midpoint plus fixed O&M (acapAt('ccgt'), acapOc('ocgt'),
acapOc('ocgd')): capacity times R/kW-yr, with no term in hours run. The LNG terminal charge (GAS_FOM_ADD, R530.5/kW-yr in c5d)
is added to BLD_FOM.ccgt and BLD_FOM.ocgt by both the pathway (the build LP) and harness/pathcheck.js (the engine check), so it
reaches CCGT and open-cycle on LNG, not open-cycle on diesel. Test ('Today 2026' at scenario year 2035, gas fuel set to R1m/MWh
so the new plant barely runs, 0.019 TWh, a 0.2% capacity factor; one headline run each, all new gas reset per case), change in
newCapexR per 1,000 MW: CCGT R3.568bn a year (R3,568/kW-yr), R4.098bn with the terminal (+R0.531bn, exactly 530.5 x 1,000 MW);
open-cycle on LNG R2.742bn, R3.273bn with the terminal; open-cycle on diesel R2.742bn, no terminal. The charge equals MW times the
R/kW-yr in every case. Harness caution found on the way: applyState resets sliders and PRESET_NON_SLIDER_KEYS only, so newOcgtMW
and newOcgdMW carry over between presets in a script; the page's optimiser leaves both at 0 (bldOcgtOn and bldOcgdOn off) and
pathcheck sets them each year, so no recorded run is affected.

Labels. Build 2026-10-16b, rendered in Chromium ('Today 2026'). No panel says energy-only. Figures that are energy-only by
construction (the hourly shadow price: the running cost of the marginal unit, and the value of lost load, R87,000/MWh, when
demand goes unserved; no capacity or reserve revenue with 'Price reserve capacity' off, the default) and how they are labelled:
- Wholesale shadow price, with its capture-price table ('what each technology actually earns': wind R755, solar R744, coal R761,
  battery R3,477/MWh): labelled 'what a market would clear at'; the footnote explains the price, not that capacity and reserve
  revenue are left out.
- Price-setting technology by hour: as above.
- Capture price forecast ('what a wind or solar PPA is worth'), capture rate by region and capture rate projections: not
  labelled energy-only; 'what a project earns' reads as total earnings.
- Battery revenue benchmark ('what a BESS would earn'): describes arbitrage in the text, not in its label.
Labelled by stream, so not energy-only and clear: battery revenue split (arbitrage, reserve and inertia, capacity; the last two
R0 by default) and battery revenue projections ('shows arbitrage only'); capacity payments (a capacity stream by design). The
shadow dynamic retail price is an all-in retail price by design and says so. Where a battery earns most needs a full model run
and was not rendered. TODO 14an bears on all of the energy-only figures: when gas runs the shadow price can sit below gas's
running cost, and storage is priced below the unit that is running, so capture prices, battery arbitrage and the missing-money
figures understate what the energy market would pay in those hours.

### The 2026 replay curtails almost nothing for oversupply; NTCSA curtailed up to 3 GW on a winter day in 2026, which the replay reaches only with every coal unit's minimum at 0.75 or more of committed capacity under the engine's commitment rules ; deemed energy for curtailed REIPPPP output is not in the engine's cost and would add at most R0.5-1.6bn a year (c5c R9.9bn, c5d R13.7bn over 2026-40) (build 2026-10-16a; user, 16 Oct 2026, messages 130 and 141 (2)); report only, no model change

Settings. 'Today 2026' preset (applyState), build 16a, harness copy at the suite's after-copy; twelve weather years (2014-2025)
times ten outage draws, the engine check's seeds (71830529 + k x 104729 + year x 7919), simulate with real profiles; the 1.3%
congestion stopgap on (congestionCurtailOn). Measured: surplus curtailment (curtailMW) and the congestion stopgap (congestMW) by
month; for May-August, each run's largest hourly surplus curtailment between 06:00 and 17:59, its largest daily total in those
hours, and the days with an hour above 1 GW. Coal minimum test (report only, local copy): every UC_FLEET row's minimum stable level
raised to at least 0.65, 0.70, 0.75 or 0.80 before the replay; nothing else changed. Script: m130_replay.js and m130_msl.js
(scratch, not in the repository).

Coal minimum stable levels in the code: the engine's 31 UC_FLEET rows across 16 stations, 15 at 0.65 and 16 at 0.50 (our own value,
unsourced, TODO 14dj), 0.563 capacity-weighted over 41,530 MW; units are committed in 4-hour blocks (BLOCK_HOURS), so a unit can come off over
midday and return for the evening peak. The build LP uses bldCoalMinFrac 0.65.

Observed (sources, no eskom.co.za):
- NTCSA: curtailment "of up to 3 000MW in a particular day" in winter 2026 (Gav Hurford, acting general manager of the System
  Operator, TechCentral, 7 Oct 2026). Sapvia: instructions to IPPs from about 100 a month earlier in 2026 to more than 1,000 a month
  (TechCentral, 15 Oct 2026; SAPVIA, 'Solar industry welcomes upfront payment of curtailment claims as IPP curtailment events climb
  tenfold', 2026).
- NTCSA's stated cause: operational constraints on the System Operator in daylight hours; coal units cannot be ramped quickly, so
  they stay online through the day at minimum stable levels to cover the morning and evening peaks; hydro and pumped storage are
  adjusted first and self-dispatching renewable IPPs are curtailed last (SAPVIA, above; Engineering News, 30 Jul 2026). This is
  oversupply against coal kept online, not a network limit. The separate congestion mechanism (NERSA, 29 Apr 2025; Western and
  Eastern Cape, 4% cap) covers grid-constrained curtailment and excludes oversupply.
- Eskom's tested minimums (user, message 141; Eskom RT&D 2023, not read here): about 44-62% of capacity without oil support.

Finding. The replay reproduces a winter peak of about 3 GW only with every unit's minimum at 0.75 or more (median run 2.5 GW, 10 of
120 runs at 3 GW or more); 0.70 gives 2.6 GW at most, 0.65 1.6 GW. That is above Eskom's tested 44-62%, so the gap is not mainly the
technical minimum: under the engine's 4-hour commitment blocks, units come off over midday, which NTCSA says the System Operator does not
do. The 0.75 floor is an effective proxy for keeping units online, not a technical minimum. Caveats: NTCSA's 3 GW is a single
reported day, not a distribution; the model has no instruction count; the 2026 replay uses the preset's fleet and the 2014-2025
weather. Implication for the 50% minimum: on its own it is within Eskom's tested range; with 4-hour decommitment it lets the engine
avoid nearly all 2026 curtailment, so the engine understates midday oversupply now and, by the same rule, in the pathway years.
This belongs with the coal flexibility option in the post-note batch (TODO 14du, message 136 (2)); no value set here.

Deemed energy (message 130 (2)). The engine does not charge for curtailed REIPPPP output: system cost pays the PPA on
delivered REIPPPP output only (reipppOutputMWh times reipppRate(year)). Deemed energy appears only in the retail panel, on
curtailment above 10% of wind and solar output system-wide (RETAIL_T curtailment_compensation), a level no year of c5c or c5d
reaches (largest 3.9%, c5d 2040). Estimate, same hooked engine check as message 135 (local copy of 16a, harness/pathcheck.js
TF=0.5 GRID=1, all years; constants read through FIXED as the engine reads them): REIPPPP's share of each hour's curtailment,
pro rata to delivered output at the engine's own REIPPPP shares (4,042 MW of the wind, 2,783 MW of the utility solar), surplus
curtailment and the 1.3% stopgap apart, valued at reipppRate(year), the average REIPPPP tariff in 2026 rands with expired
windows paying nothing. No threshold is applied, so for BW1-6, which pay only beyond a threshold, it is an upper bound. The
hooked check returns both runs' recorded engine PV and CO2 to every digit.

2026 and R1.5bn in late July, a backlog built up from April and May (Engineering News, 18 June and 27 July 2026), against R402m
of deemed energy for all of 2025 (NERSA; the basis of the 1.3% stopgap). The model's 2026 figure, R0.47bn, sits on 2025's level by
construction; 2026's claims run several times higher, in line with the oversupply curtailment the 2026 replay does not produce
(above). Caveats: the R1.5-2bn is a backlog, not a year's total; the rate averages all windows and technologies.

Build limits on new solar in c5d (yearly cap 2,500 MW in 2026 rising 7% a year to 6,446 MW in 2040):
- The yearly cap binds only in 2030: 3,277 MW built at the cap, reduced cost -R158,759 per MW against an objective coefficient of
  R9.23m per MW (the present value of its costs to 2040), 1.7%. In 2035 (394 MW built, cap 4,596) and 2040 (3,178 MW, cap 6,446)
  solar is at the margin: reduced cost 0.
- The freed-coal connection pool (rppool: connections at retired coal sites no more than the coal retired) binds in 2028-29 and
  2031-40, duals -R0.14m to -R0.29m per MW (2028 -R1.45m). It limits the connection discount, not the solar build. The per-year
  link (rpb_pv) binds in 2029, 2030 and 2036. The committed minimum (mbmin_pv) binds 2026-28.

10% margin against 0% (s_prm10_c5d, which returns c5c's build, against c5d), new MW by 2030 / 2035 / 2040: solar 6,791 / 20,657 /
33,606 against 6,791 / 13,744 / 24,672; lithium 6,666 / 13,438 / 20,678 against 3,190 / 7,872 / 12,239. Solar moves with lithium:
+8.9 GW of solar with +8.4 GW of lithium by 2040.

Tracking capacity factor. New utility solar's national tracking profile averages 28.67% over the twelve weather years (2014-2025),
27.35% to 29.58% by year. The profile is a capacity-weighted blend of regions: Northern Cape 39.2%, Limpopo 15.5%, Hydra Central
14.0%, North West 13.6%, Western Cape 11.0%, Free State 5.2%, Gauteng 1.5%; the Northern Cape alone gives 30.11%. The gap to 30.13%
is the site mix, not the weather years (no year reaches 30.13%). Correction to the request: 30.13% is BW6 bids' typical
single-axis tracking capacity factor (IPP Office REIPPPP historical data note, 7 Nov 2025, definition not stated; BW6_PV_TRK_BID_CF),
the basis on which BW7's tariffs are turned into capex; BW7's own capacity factors are not published.

Grid charges in bids (research helper, 16 Oct 2026; the web reader failed, Firecrawl read two sources before running out of
credits, the rest is search snippets; no eskom.co.za page opened):
- Shallow connection: paid by the bidder, inside the bid tariff, no cap. The bid carries a cost estimate letter from the grid
  provider (BW5 Part B 2.6.3.6.2.2; IPP Office, BW5 Bidders' Conference Queries and Clarifications, 26 May 2021, Q7, Q10, Q11, Q50,
  Q70, read; tariff adjustments only for exchange and interest rates, "any other cost items are Bidders' risk"). Cost estimate
  letters can include 400 kV shared or upstream scopes. BW7 accepts a cost estimate letter or a budget quote (Cliffe Dekker
  Hofmeyr, 7 Feb 2024, read).
- Generator use-of-system: a transmission network charge for generators in R/kW a month on maximum export capacity, in six zones;
  Cape and Karoo R0.00 in 2026/27 (tariff booklet snippet, on eskom.co.za, not opened; other zones not verified). Reimbursed to the
  seller under the PPA (BW6 wind PPA, Appendix K2, 'Use of System Charges', clause 8.4, snippet; Eberhard and Naude, REIPPPP
  Review 2017, p. 127, snippet), so not in the tariff. The clause wording seen names distribution charges; that transmission
  charges are reimbursed too is the helper's inference.
- Deep strengthening: socialised through network tariffs, not paid by bidders (Engineering News, 1 Oct 2014, snippet). No 2025
  decision found moving it onto generators; NERSA's congestion curtailment (29 Apr 2025, 4% cap, 1,580 MW in the Western and Eastern
  Cape) and the Grid Capacity Allocation Rules (27 Nov 2025) leave it there.
- Overlap with the R402/kW-yr integration charge (FIXED.txRPerKWyr, from TDP 2024 generation integration spend): small at most.
  R402 is shared-network spend bidders do not pay; the use-of-system charge is reimbursed and R0 in the Cape and Karoo. The only
  likely double count is the bidder-paid share of shared connection works in cost estimate letters, and only if TDP 2024 counts
  them; that belongs with the spur charge (bldGridCapexKW), not the R402. Not verified: the BW7 and BESIPPPP clauses, clause 8.4's
  text, the other zones' charges, and whether TDP generation integration spend includes IPP-funded works.
- Who pays the R402 in c5d (bldGridAnn, from the code): new wind, utility solar, CCGT, open-cycle on LNG and on diesel, pumped
  hydro and offshore wind, each also paying its spur annuity; batteries, flow batteries and iron-air pay none (bldGridBattHalf 0);
  rooftop pays none. s_grid0_c5d (R0 for wind and solar) and s_grid50_c5d (R201) bound its effect; reported with the c5d
  sensitivities.

Whether the panel's finding holds. The NERSA claim the checks guard: the blocks separate on the tail, not the level, and Megaflex
charges high-season off-peak above blocks that model cheaper. Pre-2025 finding, kept as recorded (windows before 1 April 2025,
measured on builds up to 2026-10-16h, last on 16h, 17 Oct 2026): every block's median within 5% of the others (1.3% on 16h;
high-season peak R754/MWh), so the blocks separated on the tail only. On the 2025/26 windows (17a) the high-season peak block
separates on its median too: R992 against R745-751 for every other block, because its 17-20 evening peak catches more of the
winter hours where coal does not set the price. The other six blocks sit within 0.8% of each other at the median. The peak blocks
now carry more of the scarcity hours (high peak mean +25%, low peak +23%) and the standard blocks less (high -20%, low -14%).
Off-peak hours are unchanged (weekday 22-06), so low-season off-peak stays the cheapest block, and the check that wants
high-season off-peak cheapest fails as it has since 14d.

The check re-specified (Nick's decision, message 183 (1)): validate_consistency's 'the blocks barely separate a typical hour'
becomes two checks, 'outside the high-season peak, the blocks barely separate a typical hour' (the other six medians within 5%;
0.8% on 17a) and 'the high-season peak separates on its median' (above every other block's median by more than 5%; 32% on 17a).
Both pass. The probe now returns each block's median by name.

Homeflex's average day, unweighted (the rates over the windows; flex in the retail panel): R2.7008/kWh on 16h, R2.5430 on 17a
(-5.8%): weekends move from weekday rates to mostly off-peak, while the evening standard hours move up from off-peak.
