R6,206/MWh). (a) Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ (June 2025), Appendix A, LCOE v18.0 key assumptions, p.37: gas peaking (new
build) 15%-10% capacity factor (read 18 Oct 2026; user, message 199 (1)); 10% is the bottom of that range. An international
gas-peaker reference, not a South African diesel figure; the caption says so (build 2026-10-17f). It replaces this note's first
version, which rested on search results only and gave newer editions as 15-20%. The c5e figures are held for the captions only (C5E_2030_*). Slider maxima
widened (lithium R8.00/kWh, diesel R20.00/kWh) so c5e's run-based costs can be set on them.

Typed and unsourced, captions say so: pumped storage R1,400, vanadium flow R2,100, iron-air R1,750, nuclear R1,650, CSP R2,000
(in the repository since its first commit, 1 Oct 2026; sources after the preset PR, TODO 14fw (2)). New coal R1,550 keeps its
source (Coal Baseload IPP Programme, bid window 1, October 2016, escalated).

The replacement-cost figure (message 194 (1)). It needs each technology's cost to the run, not at reference use: lithium and diesel
now come from the run's own capacity, priced at the slider's cost per unit of capacity (the slider times the reference output of
that capacity: 365 cycles of the run's lithium energy; 10% of the run's diesel MW), plus diesel's running cost on the energy the
run burns. The capital part is measured against the running cost the anchor was built on, so the fuel and carbon sliders move only
the running cost. Vanadium flow and iron-air stay priced per MWh discharged at their typed LCOE, on their share of the battery
class's energy; every other technology stays energy x LCOE. At the page's defaults the figure goes from R1,532.8 to R1,604.5/MWh
(+4.7%); on c5e's 2030 fleet (4,666 MW of new lithium at 2.95 h, 8,206 MW wind, 7,339 MW solar, 3,600 MW rooftop) from R1,317.5
to R1,443.5 (+9.6%).

### Avon and Dedisa's must-run in the build LP capped at the independent peakers' diesel, as the engine does (build 2026-10-17b): c5e's pass-1 LP unchanged (key b7e3107906); the Fossil-free B start's LP equals its must-run-off run; no recorded run affected (user, 17 Oct 2026, message 182 (2); TODO 14fk)

The change. The build LP's mdr_ row now forces min(the must-run, the independent peakers' diesel standing that year): existing
diesel (DSL(y), after diesel retirements and any peaker retirement schedule) less Eskom's own tank-fed plant (FIXED.dslTankMW), the
engine's rule in simulate ('_mdIpp'). Before, the row had no cap, so retiring diesel below the must-run level before Avon's
contract ends (20 July 2031) made the LP infeasible. One difference remains: the engine's dieselAvailMW also counts new diesel
open-cycle plant, which in the LP is a decision variable and is left out of the cap; it matters only when the independent
peakers' existing diesel falls below the must-run level before 2031 and new diesel open-cycle is built, which no recorded run does.

  17b with no switch, against the same on the frozen 16h copy with the must-run off (MDR_OFF, scratch): key fd5b75b684 on both,
  the LP files byte-identical; no mdr_ rows, since all diesel is retired. So the B start that ran on 16h with MDR_OFF is what the
  fixed LP gives.

check, preset or replay is affected.

The change. 'IRP's 2030 targets', 'IRP's 2030 targets, grid delayed' and 'IRP path 2035' now read coalDecomMW from the per-unit
dates the pathway uses as COAL_DATES (harness/coal_dates_irp2025.json: Nick Hedley's reading of Figure 3, plan p.12, 13 Oct 2026,
50-year line, about +-250 MW), through irpFig3CoalRetiredMW, with the summation and scaling of bldCoalMW (rule 3). The page loads
the file at start-up; the page's own coal schedule (UC_FLEET's dates) is unchanged (probe: 30,296 MW standing at the start of 2030
either way; Figure 3 gives 32,433). Probe on this build: 7,259 MW retired by the start of 2030, 13,776 MW by the start of 2035.

Why the numbers differ from the typed ones. The IRP's "8 GW by 2030" (plan p.40) is an end state, the units named to close by the
financial year 2030; Figure 3 is an annual average, so the coal standing through 2030 is higher than at its end. No IRP source was
found for 16,000 MW by 2035: the preset's comment based it on the MTSAO's "about 17 GW of coal and gas out by 2035", which
is not coal alone.

Moves against today: main's Deep, retail +R1.087/kWh (+28.7%) and system cost +R0.310/kWh (+28.2%); the new Deep +R0.553
(+14.6%) and +R0.030 (+2.7%); Fossil-free +R1.867 (+49.4%) and +R0.392 (+35.6%). The near-equal percentages on main's Deep
were a ratio of the two bases (the retail price is about 3.4 times the system cost), not a property: in every case the panel
rises by several times as much in rand. What the panel carries and system cost does not, on the new Deep at cost level: coal's
stranded and existing capital (+R0.110/kWh; system cost leaves sunk capital out by design, RESULTS 'Sunk capital stays out');
the network over 4.3% fewer kWh sold (+R0.063; rooftop takes sales); IPP contracts at their 2026 payments (unchanged) where
the 2035 engine has retired part of them (REIPPPP -R0.090, other IPP -R0.039); new-build capital at 2026 prices per kWh sold
(R0.894 with the new grid) against the engine's 2035 capital per MWh served (R0.804). Fuel (-R0.456 against -R0.455) and
fixed O&M (-R0.136 against -R0.156) fall alike. With the panel set to 2035 the IPP term matches and the gap narrows: retail
R3.329 to R3.674 (+10.4%) against system cost +2.7%. Not a bug: two different measures. The new Deep's system cost barely
rises because coal's fuel and fixed O&M almost pay for its new build by 2035.
Caveat: the searches and the top-up ran before c5f's base changes (Msenge's wind and wheeled load in demand, PR #80); on c5f's
build the presets would be rescored.

request; annual sums only, the analysis ours, not Eskom's): FY2026 thermal generation 165.38 TWh, within 0.03% of the report's
coal-fired 165,431 GWh, so the report's coal figure is on the portal's sent-out basis.

The model's factor (message 217 (a)). FIXED.emisCoal = 1.04 t CO2 per MWh sent out (CO2, not CO2e). The engine applies it to
coalFuelMWh, coal output scaled by the part-load heat-rate multiplier, so c5f's effective factor in 2026 is 1.0672 (1.04 x
1.0262) and 1.058-1.074 over 2026-40. The same constant sets coal's carbon-tax cost in the engine and the build LP (MCcoal =
costCoal + vomCoal + carbon price x emisCoal). Its source is not recorded: a code comment calls it Eskom's per-sent-out figure;
SOURCES records only Meridian's fleet file, 1.008 capacity-weighted (TODO 14gp).

Eskom's implied factor: 184.5 Mt over 165.38 TWh is 1.1156 t CO2e/MWh sent out; less Eskom's own open-cycle output (0.81 TWh at
the model's 0.78) it is 1.1118; on a CO2 basis about 1.107 (less 0.45% for CH4 and N2O: IPCC 2006 defaults for coal in energy
industries, 1 kg CH4 and 1.5 kg N2O per TJ against about 95 t CO2, at AR5's 28 and 265). Coal burnt per MWh sent out: 0.584 t.

The lines sum to -23.2 TWh against the -22.8 TWh coal gap (0.4 TWh is congestion loss and rounding). Causes, largest first:
- Renewables and imports (-15.5 TWh): c5f runs its whole 2026 fleet from 1 January, including the wheeled private wind and
  solar Eskom does not meter and the 2026 committed floors (1,131 MW of wind, 1,018 MW of solar; new wind alone 4.1 TWh); its
  existing wind gives 14.8 TWh against the portal's 11.6 (the wind benchmark's documented x1.26 on capacity, SOURCES); imports
  run at the measured April-August 2026 mean (1,066 MW).
- Exports (-7.9 TWh): c5f carries firm exports only (6.6 TWh); the portal's FY2026 exports are 14.5 TWh, falling to about
  8.7 TWh on the 2026 trend.
- Domestic load (-1.4 TWh), and nuclear, open-cycle and pumped storage (+2.0 TWh together).
- Calendar against financial year: Eskom's own coal is falling, 170.4 TWh in calendar 2025 and about 153.9 TWh for calendar 2026
  on the Jan-Aug trend (-9.7%); against that, c5f's 2026 coal gap is -11.4 TWh, not -22.8.

2026-40: +66.4 Mt on CO2e (+59.0 on CO2). Carbon-tax payments in engine PV: +R2.54bn (+R2.25bn on CO2), against c5f's R61.1bn
and its engine PV of R2,255.1bn. The engine's carbon cost per coal MWh rises by about R2.1 at 2026's R46/t and R2.8 from 2030 at
R61.3/t. In the build LP coal's marginal cost rises by the same R2-3/MWh, about 0.4% of R546 fuel + R80 VOM + carbon: the merit
order does not change (coal stays far below gas and above wind and solar), and the value of displacing coal rises by that 0.4%.
A build could move only at the margin: s_carbonfull's R410.5/t from 2030 adds about R370/MWh to coal and cut CO2 by 245.5 Mt, and
a linear reading of that puts the corrected factor at under 2 Mt and a few hundred MW; only a run would say. Not run.

  forecast, -25% for storage by 2035, about 3.1% a year over 2026-35 (3% gives -24%); no source for 5% is recorded (SOURCES
  'Lithium capex decline', TODO 14cw). Proposal: decl 0.03 in BLD_COST with the BNEF citation, BATT_DECL kept only for
  sensitivities (s_batt5 runs 5%).
- LNG terminal charge. Code: none on the page; BLD_FOM.ccgt is R462/kW-yr and the page's gas fuel default (costCcgt R2,003/MWh,
  USD 18.50/MMBtu delivered) already carries USD 2/MMBtu for regasification and transport. Pathway: GAS_CASE=central with
  GAS_FOM_ADD=530.5 (pathway_perfail.js), added to BLD_FOM.ccgt and BLD_FOM.ocgt for new gas in the optimiser, recorded as
  P.gas.fomAdd and applied by pathcheck.js, with the central fuel price R1,298.42/MWh (public_data/gas_price_cases.json). Sourced:
  the range, R354-707/kW-yr on the send-out basis (SOURCES 'Gas price cases': Ngqura, Richards Bay, Standard Bank and ENN terminal
  costs at 8% over 25 years); 530.5 is its midpoint, a choice rather than a figure from a source. Proposal: one page constant for
  the terminal charge, read by the engine's gas fixed O&M and the optimiser alike, GAS_FOM_ADD defaulting to it; and the page's
  gas fuel default moved to the central case's R1,298.42 with it, since adding the terminal to R2,003 would count regasification

  gas assumptions text, the fuel slider's note and the gas LCOE note read their figures from the code. lcoeCcgt, derived from
  costCcgt, moves from R3,201 to R2,496/MWh.

  adding to BLD_FOM, and records the decline and terminal it used (battDecl, gas.fomAdd) whether or not they were given.
  pathcheck.js sets the run's terminal (0 included) and decline; a run that recorded none (before 19b without BATT_DECL, or before
  09f without gas settings) needs BATT_DECL, or GAS_FUEL_R and GAS_FOM_ADD, to be checked as built, and is refused otherwise.
  validate_inputs adds three checks: the central case's fuel cost recomputed from its coast price, regasification and exchange
  rate; costCcgt equal to it in every year; the terminal equal to the range's midpoint.

Two corrections to the wording given. The 51% is an annual minimum capacity factor on the first 6 GW of gas (FIXED's comment:
IRP 2025, Gazette 53596, p.34; simulateGasAnnualFloor tops gas up in the highest net-load hours until the year's output reaches
it), so "load factor or more" became "an annual capacity factor of at least 51%". "Demand 27% above 2026" leaves out the 930 MW
smelter block both 2035 presets carry: growth is 26.7% on the 2026 profile (203.5 TWh), and with the block 2035 demand is 30.7%
above 2026, so the caption adds "plus 930 MW of smelter load".

### Check: how much load Today 2026 can add and still meet the reliability standard, against Eskom's claim of 3-5 GW of overcapacity: about 4 GW flat, 6 GW or more in daylight hours (build 2026-10-19e; user, 19 Oct 2026, message 243; a check, not for the note until Nick decides)

Settings. Today 2026 on build 2026-10-19e (imports 0.927, the synchronous floor reading the scenario's imports), with an added
load block from 0 to 6 GW in 500 MW steps: flat, every hour (demandBlockMW); and daytime, the same MW from 08:00 to 16:59 only,
added to the demand series passed to the engine (no engine change: the engine's block is flat, so this is a stand-in for a load
that can switch off outside daylight). Twelve weather years x 20 independent outage draws, 240 runs per block (seeds 71830529 +
k x 104729 + year x 7919, as the preset checks). The standard is 0.002% of customer demand, the block included (load less
storage charging, as harness/ext/preset_rescore.js); half of it is the presets' target. harness/ext/overcap_check.js, results
harness/ext/overcap_19e.json. The claim (Bloomberg, Oct 2026) is quoted as given to the model, not read here.

| Block, MW | Flat: shed, GWh (standard) | Worst year | Added cost, R bn | Added CO2, Mt | Daytime: shed, GWh (standard) | Worst year | Added cost | Added CO2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0.016 (3.93) | 0.15 | - | - | 0.016 (3.93) | 0.15 | - | - |
| 1,000 | 0.051 (4.10) | 0.60 | 5.88 | 8.93 | 0.042 (3.99) | 0.48 | 2.17 | 3.31 |
| 2,000 | 0.250 (4.28) | 2.38 | 11.90 | 17.74 | 0.092 (4.06) | 0.78 | 4.40 | 6.64 |
| 3,000 | 0.939 (4.45) | 5.39 | 18.24 | 26.40 | 0.225 (4.12) | 1.68 | 6.69 | 9.93 |
| 3,500 | 2.020 (4.54) | 8.71 | 21.67 | 30.67 | 0.321 (4.16) | 2.08 | 7.86 | 11.55 |
| 4,000 | 4.195 (4.63) | 15.75 | 25.38 | 34.91 | 0.503 (4.19) | 2.68 | 9.08 | 13.14 |
| 4,500 | 8.719 (4.72), fails | 26.65 | 29.52 | 39.12 | 0.778 (4.22) | 3.33 | 10.37 | 14.71 |
| 5,000 | 17.739 (4.80), fails | 44.60 | 34.19 | 43.31 | 1.284 (4.26) | 4.43 | 11.75 | 16.27 |
| 5,500 | 34.043 (4.89), fails | 70.28 | 39.58 | 47.45 | 2.160 (4.29) | 6.05 | 13.27 | 17.80 |

- Flat: the largest block that meets the standard is 4,000 MW (4.20 GWh against 4.63; 4,500 MW sheds 8.72 against 4.72); at
  half the standard, 3,500 MW (2.02 against 2.27). Serving 4 GW adds 35.0 TWh a year at R25.4bn and 34.9 Mt: R725/MWh and
  1.00 t/MWh, coal at the margin. The worst weather year sheds 15.75 GWh, 3.4 times the year's standard.
- Daytime (08:00-16:59): every block to 6,000 MW meets the standard (3.60 GWh against 4.32); at half the standard, 5,000 MW.
  6 GW in daylight adds 19.6 TWh at R15.0bn and 19.3 Mt: R763/MWh and 0.98 t/MWh.
- Caveats: one year's fleet (Today 2026's coal availability and outage model), the engine's dispatch rather than Eskom's; the
  added cost is system cost (fuel, start-up, carbon and the like), not a tariff; 500 MW steps, so the flat limit lies between 4.0
  and 4.5 GW. Recorded as a check; not for the note until Nick decides.

### The rooftop tab's satellite map opened on 'Map data not yet available' tiles after a rural or offshore site query; it now opens only as deep as Esri has imagery; the tab's default tariff is Businessrate 3 (build 2026-10-19f; user, 19 Oct 2026, messages 248 and 249)

Cause. rtInitMap opened the map at zoom 19 on the last site-query location (window._resourceData) and rtGoTo went to 19 on an
address result; Esri's World Imagery reaches 19 in cities but often only 18 in rural areas and offshore, and where a zoom has no
imagery Esri serves 'Map data not yet available' tiles rather than an error. Esri's tilemap service, at four points (data 1 =
imagery at that zoom): Sandton 16-19 all 1; near De Aar (-30.65, 24.0), offshore Eastern Cape (-34.2, 25.8) and near Beaufort
West (-32.5, 22.3) 16-18 1, 19 0.

Fix. rtImageryZoom asks the tilemap service for the deepest zoom up to 19 at a point (cached per location; null and uncached if
the service cannot be reached); rtShowAt opens at zoom 17, then goes as deep as there is imagery, and caps the imagery layer's
native zoom there, so a deeper view enlarges real imagery; the cap is re-checked at the centre after a pan or zoom. A fresh load
with no site still opens at 16 over Johannesburg; an address result goes to 19 where Esri has it.

Render check (Chromium, fresh page per case; harness/render/2026-10-19f/, render_rtmap.js). The site query (Open-Meteo) and the
address search (Nominatim) cannot be reached from the test container, so the cases set what each sets when it succeeds:
window._resourceData = {lat, lng}, and rtGoTo(lat, lng, true). Of the 12 imagery tiles shown, how many Esri's tilemap service
says have imagery:

| Case | Before (main, 19d): zoom, tiles with imagery | After (19f): zoom, tiles with imagery |
|---|---|---|
| Fresh load, no site | 16, 12 of 12 | 16, 12 of 12 |
| Site query near De Aar | 19, 0 of 12 ('Map data not yet available') | 18, 12 of 12 |
| Site query 20 km off the Eastern Cape coast | 19, 0 of 12 | 18, 12 of 12 (sea) |
| Johannesburg address (Sandton City) | 19, 12 of 12 | 19, 12 of 12 |

No page errors in any case.

The tab's default customer (message 248, decided in 249). The defaults, a R80,000 monthly bill at R2.50/kWh, are a business
customer's; they predate the repository (build 2026-10-01a). Decided: keep a business default, as the tab sits with the project
tools (249 (1)); replace the unsourced R2.50/kWh with Eskom's Businessrate 3, non-local authority, 2026/27 (Tariffs and Charges
Booklet 2026/2027, p.23), excluding VAT, which a business reclaims (249 (2)): energy 242.90, ancillary service 0.45, network demand
15.81, and electrification and rural network subsidy 5.37 c/kWh, 264.53 in all; network capacity R81.98, service and
administration R15.99 and generation capacity R11.18 per point of delivery a day, R109.15 in all. One constant
(RT_BIZRATE3_2026) holds the seven charges; the default tariff is computed from them as the all-in rate at the default bill
(RT_DEFAULT_BILL, R80,000): the fixed R3,320 a month spread over the 28,986 kWh the rest of the bill buys, R2.76/kWh. The bill and
tariff fields read the two constants (each was typed three times), and a note under the tariff field gives the source.

What moves at the tab's defaults (2,000 m2 roof, 331.1 kWp, the national solar average):

| At the defaults | R2.50/kWh | Businessrate 3, R2.76/kWh |
|---|---|---|
| Estimated use | 32,000 kWh a month | 28,986 |
| Generation against the site's annual use | 1.1 times | 1.3 times |
| Self-consumed share of generation | 58% | 54% (188 MWh a year exported, no credit; was 162) |
| Annual savings | R635k | R647k |
| Simple payback | 6.3 years | 6.2 |
| IRR, 25 years at 5% escalation | 21.3% | 21.6% |
| NPV at 10% | R4.7m | R4.9m |

Savings rise 1.9% on a tariff 10.4% higher: the same bill buys fewer kWh, so more of the system's output is exported unpaid.
For Nick: the tab's one tariff does two jobs, turning the bill into kWh (where the all-in rate is right) and valuing solar used on
site (where the variable rate, R2.6453, is right, since fixed charges do not fall with solar); at the default bill the two differ
by 4.3%.

Not changed (249 (2)): the C&I pre-feasibility module's 'Avg industrial tariff 2026 ≈ R2.50/kWh' is a larger customer's and does
not share Businessrate 3, which is for supplies up to 100 kVA. Megaflex (booklet p.13) is the tariff for it, but pricing an
average needs a reference customer: transmission zone, supply voltage, a load shape across Eskom's time-of-use periods and
seasons, and the per-kVA network and capacity charges (for example, at 500 V to 66 kV within 300 km, energy runs from 120.03 c/kWh
off-peak to 720.19 peak in the high season, plus R12.27/kVA a month of generation capacity and R39.13 and R26.29/kVA of
network capacity and demand). Proposed for Nick to choose.

### Site speed, step 1 and 2: stored risk panels, a session cache, panels computed only on screen and cancelled when a control moves; a fresh load is free in 4 s instead of 55, a preset click in 0.5-2.2 s instead of 37-201 s; no figure changes (build 2026-10-19g; user, 19 Oct 2026, messages 226, 242, 251, 254-256)

What changed (index.html; branch claude/site-speed):
- Stored risk panels. stored_panels.json holds the Monte Carlo risk panel, the adequacy board and the capture curve for the
  start-up state and every preset, computed by the page's own code (harness/validate_stored_panels.js --write). The page uses
  an entry only for the exact scenario (every key of state, FIXED and whether the measured profiles loaded) and only while its
  fingerprint matches: a hash of the page's scripts as parsed and of the nine start-up engine files as they arrive.
- Session cache: panels and main results computed live are kept for the session (main results as a copy taken before anything
  draws on them, since drawDispatch adds stack.curtailment to the result; up to eight scenarios).
- Panels run only when on screen (IntersectionObserver): Monte Carlo, adequacy, capture curve, heat stress, and the external
  comparison, which sits in a closed section yet ran the engine twice on every change. A panel owed while off screen is dimmed.
  Without IntersectionObserver (old browsers, the test harnesses) every panel counts as on screen, as before.
- A control that moves cancels the panel runs in flight before their next draw (one draw at a time, was 12 and 8).
- The first capture curve, and the other panels, wait until every engine input has settled (TODO 14ds (e)).
- The weather-year files load once for both ensembles; the 9 MB weather file is no longer fetched at start-up for the P50/P90
  table, which fills only after a site query.

At four times slower the branch's clicks freeze 2.4 to 11.0 s (IRP path 2035 the longest). Step 1 alone (the branch with
IntersectionObserver removed, normal speed): fresh load free 8.5 s, longest 3.6 s; clicks 2.6 to 11.4 s, because heat stress
and the external comparison still ran in every run(). After a slider move the risk panel computes live, one draw per task, so
the page stays usable but the panel takes as long as before; the web worker (251 (3)) is what moves that work off the page.

Checks.
- validate_stored_panels.js (86 checks, in the suite): every stored panel equals a fresh computation to the digit for the
  start-up state and all eight presets; the fingerprint matches; each file the panels were computed from is unchanged; the page
  draws the stored panels exactly as fresh ones; a revisit from the session cache draws every element as a fresh run; and the
  main results are identical whether or not the weather years have loaded (the stored panels mean they may never load).
- On the preview (verify.js): the page used the stored panels with no live draw; stored_panels.json is 85 kB raw, 15.5 kB as
  Cloudflare serves it (zstd), and arrived 1.4-1.8 s into the load, before the panels needed it; profiles.json served with one
  trailing space (same numbers, different file) made the fingerprint miss and the panels compute live; a preset then one slider
  moved: the preset from the store, then the risk panel live; a reload after moving a slider restores the scenario from the URL,
  no stored entry matches, and the panels compute live.
- Found and fixed while checking: the page first hashed its scripts when asked, so a script added later (an extension, a test
  harness) changed the fingerprint; it now hashes them once when parsing ends. On main, the board's last word was the adequacy
  ensemble's because the two runs alternated draw by draw; the stored panels keep that order (Monte Carlo, then adequacy).
- The site review's B3 (two ensembles writing the board) is timing only: no change (recorded in the review file with batch 2).

Rule from this (message 255 (4)): every pull request that changes index.html regenerates stored_panels.json (RULES.md, HANDOVER).
Writing takes about 20 minutes, the check about 25.

### A link or a reload with new wind never computed; a link now runs only after every start-up file has loaded, and carries the preset (build 2026-10-20e, with #98's web worker merged in; user, 20 Oct 2026, messages 263 (1) and 265, from the mechanics audit G1-M1)

Cause (reproduced in Chromium on main 38edbbb): the page ran the engine once while it was still loading (an early run on
the synthetic profiles, for first numbers). A link's scenario was applied before that run, so with new wind the run called the
modern wind map before nodal/profiles_wind_modern_map.json had loaded and threw ('modern wind is on but
nodal/profiles_wind_modern_map.json is not loaded'); the throw stopped the rest of the page's start-up, so GTZA_READY never
came and the page never computed. ?newWindMW=1000: not computed after 90 s; ?newPvMW=1000: computed in 3.4 s. A link also
carried slider values only (and a link's 0 read as the slider's default), so a 2035 preset reopened at 2026.

What changed (index.html):
- A link that carries a scenario skips the early run; its scenario runs once every start-up file has loaded. The early run, on
  a plain visit, can no longer stop the start-up (caught and logged).
- ?preset=<name> applies the preset as a click does (every non-slider key, the year included), then any slider values in the
  link on top. The page remembers the preset a scenario started from (basePreset), so after a click the address carries the
  preset and only the sliders that differ from it; moving a slider keeps the preset in the address.
- A link's 0 is kept; select controls are read from links too.

After, in Chromium on this branch: ?newWindMW=1000 computed in 2.5 s; ?preset=IRP path 2035 in 4.6 s at 2035; ?preset=
Fossil-free 2040&demandGrowthPct=10 in 2.4 s at 2040; a plain visit in 3.4 s.

New check, harness/validate_links.js (48 checks, about 5 minutes, in the suite list): for every preset, a fresh ?preset= link
and a reload of the address a click leaves each equal the click (every key of state, and every number of simulate's result,
hashed); a preset then a slider moved, reloaded, equals the two steps by hand and stays at 2035; ?newWindMW=1000 and
?newPvMW=1000 compute and equal the start-up page with the slider moved. 48/48 on this branch. On main 38edbbb, 13/39 (a page
that never computes skips its comparison): the reload after a click throws the wind-map error on six of the eight presets (every
preset with new wind), as the audit found; the ?preset= links reproduce nothing; ?newWindMW=1000 never computes.

The web worker (#98, merged into this branch from main) has no start-up run of its own: its first full run waits for the worker,
which starts after every start-up file has loaded; the guarded early run above is the only one before that (message 265).

### Rooftop output against sbg.earth (report only): the 2026 replay gives 15.4 TWh a year after losses against sbg.earth's about 12.9 TWh; about two thirds of the 2.5 TWh gap is the 2025 solar profile running above its twelve-year mean, the rest within the capacity and derate figures (user, 22 Oct 2026, message 317 (a); build 2026-10-22a)

Settings: Today 2026 as the page applies it, simulate on the page's own profiles (profiles.json, calendar 2025), jsdom; script
scratch roof317.js. Rooftop capacity 8,942.1 MW (FIXED.rooftopMW, no new rooftop in 2026). The engine's rooftop output each hour is
capacity x the national solar profile x rooftopDerate (0.78), capped at 90% of that hour's demand (index.html, simulate).

| Step | TWh a year | Capacity factor |
|---|---|---|
| Capacity x 2025 profile, before losses | 19.69 | 25.1% |
| After the 0.78 derate (the engine's output; the 90% demand cap never binds) | 15.36 | 19.6% |
| Capacity x the twelve-year mean (FIXED_PV_CF_12Y 0.224), before losses | 17.54 | 22.4% |
| Twelve-year mean after the derate | 13.69 | 17.5% |
| sbg.earth's estimate | about 12.9 | about 16.5% on 8,942 MW |

The one loss is the derate, 0.78 (orientation, shading, soiling, inverter and export limiting; FIXED.rooftopDerate, status
'sourced (by name, unconfirmed)' in the register). The gap is real in the replay: the 2025 profile is Eskom's metered utility-
scale fleet, which ran at 25.1% that year against its twelve-year mean of 22.4% (a sunnier year or more tracking plant in the
fleet; the split is not measured here), so rooftop inherits about 1.7 TWh it would not get on a typical year. On the twelve-year mean the model gives 13.7 TWh,
6% above sbg.earth; that remainder is within the uncertainty of the installed capacity (sbg.earth's own capacity figure is not
known here) and of the derate. The derate's code comment aims at 17.5%, which holds only on the twelve-year mean. Caveat:
sbg.earth's method and capacity are not checked (SOURCES 'Leads from a SAPVIA spokesperson's deck').

### Coal marginal cost's rand year, a sensitivity: indexing PyPSA-RSA's marginal_cost from 2024 rands to 2026 raises the average price 1-6% on the four note presets, from 2023 rands 2-11%; dispatch, system cost and CO2 unchanged (build 2026-10-20f, main 51150a8; user, 20 Oct 2026, message 268 (5); measure only, no model change until Meridian answers, TODO 14hu)

Why: PyPSA-RSA states no currency year (config.yaml at commit 89872c1: USD_to_ZAR 18.24, EUR_to_ZAR 17.83, no year given,
checked 20 Oct 2026; the user reads the ME IRP 2024 workbook's coal fuel series as rising to 2024 and flat after). The model
uses UC_FLEET's marginal_cost as 2026 rands. If they are 2023 or 2024 rands, the coal price is understated by the CPI since.

Settings: every marginal_cost in UC_FLEET and MIP_FLEET (62 values; Arnot* R664.14) multiplied by the factor in the page text
before load; each preset as a click applies it (applyState(PRESETS[name])), simulate(state, PROFILES) in jsdom; script
scratchpad cpi/mc.js. Factors, January to January, Stats SA headline CPI as already used in the model (SOURCES 'SA CPI,
January 2024 to January 2026'; 5.3% y/y January 2024 as in BLD_COST's wind_high note): 2024 rands x 1.032 x 1.035 = 1.0681
(CPI_JAN24_TO_JAN26); 2023 rands x 1.053 x 1.0681 = 1.1247. The Stats SA site is not reachable from the cloud environment,
so the rates are as reported, not read from the P0141 tables; an annual-average basis would differ slightly. R/MWh, mean of
the 8,760 hourly prices; coal-set price is the mean over hours whose marginalTech is 'coal'.

| Preset | Average price: as now / 2024 rands / 2023 rands | Coal-set price: as now / 2024 / 2023 | Coal-set hours (coal at a negative price, not counted) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Today 2026 | 677.3 / 719.2 (+6.2%) / 754.1 (+11.3%) | 665.8 / 707.8 / 742.7 | 8,730 (0) |
| IRP's 2030 targets | 1,006.4 / 1,025.3 (+1.9%) / 1,041.1 (+3.4%) | 686.0 / 728.1 / 763.1 | 3,115 (295) |
| IRP path 2035 | 880.3 / 888.2 (+0.9%) / 894.7 (+1.6%) | 681.5 / 723.3 / 758.0 | 1,218 (781) |
| Least-cost path 2035 | 701.1 / 734.7 (+4.8%) / 762.5 (+8.8%) | 676.9 / 718.5 / 753.0 | 5,394 (224) |

Dispatch (every hour of every technology, hashed), system cost and CO2 are identical in all three: the merit order within coal
is unchanged by a common factor, and the system cost prices coal from FIXED.costCoal, not from marginal_cost. Only what reads
the hourly price moves (capture prices, storage revenue, the shadow retail price, the price panel). The effect is smallest on
IRP path 2035, where coal sets the price in 1,218 hours. Caveat: the price is the model's shadow price, not a market price;
start-up costs (startup_cost) carry the same unknown year and were not indexed here.

### Site review batch 2: display logic and small code fixes on 17 findings; Deep decarbonisation 2035 rescored on outage patterns it was not chosen on, 1.49 GWh a year against 2.42 (build 2026-10-19i; user, 19 Oct 2026, message 252)

Each finding was confirmed in the code on build 2026-10-19f before it was changed (site review of 19 Oct 2026, Nick's copy).

A1 (Deep's reliability claimed out of sample). Deep decarbonisation 2035 was topped up on the outage draws of seed 71830529
and then scored on the same draws, so its 2.27 GWh was in sample. Rescored on build 19i on a fresh, disjoint seed set:
`SEED=120000017 ONLY=Deep VARIANTS=page node harness/ext/preset_rescore.js` (twelve weather years x 20 draws, seeds
120000017 + k x 104729 + year x 7919; output harness/ext/rescore_page_19i_deep_fresh.json, 128 s). Mean unserved 1.49 GWh a
year against a target of 2.42 (half the 0.002% standard on customer demand), cost R318.2bn, CO2 16.0 Mt: it meets the
target out of sample. PRESET_SCORES now takes each preset from its own rescore (gen_preset_scores.py): Deep from the fresh
run, Fossil-free 2040 from 19e's (it had no top-up, so its draws were never used to choose it). The caption's 'outage patterns
it was not chosen on' is now true for both. Caveat: 1.49 on fresh draws against 2.27 on the tuning draws is a wide gap for 240
runs each; the score is a mean over few rare shortfall events.

### The rooftop tab took system losses three times; it now takes them once, and yields at the defaults rise 20-45% (build 2026-10-19j; user, 19 Oct 2026, message 252, site review A47)

Cause (confirmed in the code on build 2026-10-19f): rtCalc multiplied the site's capacity factor, which already carries the
system losses (Open-Meteo yield at a performance ratio of 0.80; the 0.21 fallback is PVGIS with its losses), by 'Shading &
losses' (default 0.80) and again by a per-type 'system/inverter' factor (usagePct, 0.80 to 0.90).

What changed (index.html, rtCalc and RT_TYPES): the capacity factor carries the system losses; the control is shading only
(messages 260 (5) and 261 (1)): Minimal 100%, no shading beyond the base yield's losses, because the base already carries 20%
(a performance ratio of 0.80), above PVWatts' 14% default total, which includes its 3% shading (A. P. Dobos, 'PVWatts Version 5
Manual', NREL/TP-6A20-62641, 2014; pvlib's pvwatts_losses); Moderate 93%, the default, and Heavy 85%: our assumptions, applied
to the base and labelled so on the control. usagePct is removed. The 0.21
fallback is PVGIS at a tilt equal to the latitude, so it is divided by the 25-degree orientation factor (1.08) to bring it to a
flat roof before the orientation control applies, since that control is relative to flat.

Before (build 2026-10-19f, main) and after (2026-10-19j), every other control at its default (typical obstructions, flat roof,
15-degree north orientation, 5% escalation, no battery, default bill and tariff); 'fallback' is no site queried, 'site' a site
whose capacity factor is 20%. Computed by rtCalc itself in jsdom (scratchpad b1/rt.js), read from window._rtSheet:

| Roof area, bracket | Case | kWp | CF before / after | Yield MWh/yr before / after | Savings R k/yr before / after | Payback yr before / after |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 60 m2, home | fallback | 9.9 | 17.6% / 19.0% | 14 / 16 | 13 / 16 | 15.8 / 12.7 |
| 400 m2, small C&I | fallback | 65.7 | 17.6% / 19.0% | 89 / 109 | 134 / 165 | 7.0 / 5.6 |
| 2,000 m2, large C&I | fallback | 331.1 | 17.6% / 19.0% | 435 / 551 | 647 / 671 | 6.2 / 5.9 |
| 12,000 m2, industrial | fallback | 1,989.6 | 17.6% / 19.0% | 2,460 / 3,309 | 682 / 682 | 47.5 / 47.5 |
| 60 m2, home | site 20% | 9.9 | 16.8% / 19.5% | 13 / 17 | 13 / 16 | 16.8 / 12.3 |
| 400 m2, small C&I | site 20% | 65.7 | 16.8% / 19.5% | 85 / 112 | 128 / 169 | 7.4 / 5.5 |
| 2,000 m2, large C&I | site 20% | 331.1 | 16.8% / 19.5% | 414 / 566 | 641 / 672 | 6.2 / 5.9 |
| 12,000 m2, industrial | site 20% | 1,989.6 | 16.8% / 19.5% | 2,342 / 3,404 | 682 / 682 | 47.5 / 47.5 |

The same cases at Minimal shading (100%) on this build, re-measured 20 Oct 2026 (the 'before' build's Minimal was 85% for
shading and losses together, so it has no like-for-like column): CF 20.4% (fallback) and 21.0% (site); yield 18, 118, 592 and
3,558 MWh/yr (fallback) and 18, 121, 609 and 3,660 (site); savings R17k, 177k, 675k and 682k (fallback) and 17k, 182k, 677k and
682k (site); payback 11.7, 5.2, 5.9 and 47.5 years (fallback) and 11.3, 5.1, 5.9 and 47.5 (site), in the table's order.

The CF column is after orientation and shading (the yield is kWp x CF x 8,760, after usagePct before). The industrial case does

Source: Meridian Economics, 'Renewable Energy Levelised Cost Tool', June 2020, Table 1, p.iii: degradation 0.3% a year for wind,
0.5% for solar PV (SOURCES 'Meridian Economics'). Arithmetic: levelised output at 8% real over 25 years (BLD_LIFE wind and pv),
degradation from year 2: -2.42% (wind), -3.99% (solar); from year 1: -2.71% and -4.47% (the user's 2.4% and 4.0% confirmed).

| | Wind | Tracking solar |
|---|---|---|
| Levelised output, degradation from year 2 | -2.42% | -3.99% |
| Capex backed out of the tariff without degradation (c5e, 'run') | R20,879/kW | R11,038/kW |
| The same with degradation | R20,272/kW (-2.9%) | R10,476/kW (-5.1%) |
| Cost per MWh on 'run' (capex backed out and dispatch both without degradation) | the tariff, R630.6 | the tariff, R526.1 |
| Cost per MWh with capex held ('bid', c5d), degradation added | +2.48% | +4.15% |

On 'run' the model leaves degradation out of both the capex derivation and the dispatch, so the two cancel in the cost per MWh;
what is wrong is per MW: lifetime output per MW too high, so too little capacity for a given energy, more so as plant ages, and
capex per kW too high. Adding degradation to the capex derivation only gives R615.3 (wind) and R505.1/MWh (solar), which mixes two
treatments. On 'bid' (c5d), capex is fixed, so cost per MWh was understated by 2.5% and 4.2%.

stated), against the model's 42.5% and 28.7%; wind and solar levelised cost about a third lower by 2040 (Figure 1, p.v; NREL
ATB 2019 learning), against the model's 3.89% a year solar capex decline, 43% lower by 2040, which has no source.

Definition (EirGrid, as in Beyond Fossil Fuels, Ember, E3G and IEEFA, May 2025, p.21; Ireland's limit 75%, Figure 4, p.22;
SOURCES): non-synchronous generation plus HVDC imports, over demand plus exports. Counted here, hour by hour: non-synchronous =
wind, utility solar, rooftop, RMIPPPP hybrids, battery and flow-storage discharge, and imports (Cahora Bassa arrives by HVDC);
synchronous = coal, nuclear, hydro, pumped storage, CSP, gas and diesel. Demand = the engine's grid load with storage charging
(charging on the demand side) and firm exports, plus rooftop (gross demand, since rooftop counts as generation), plus surplus
exports. Unserved energy stays in demand.

Cause: with lithium held to 550 MW a year, solar loses most of the storage that moves its output into the evening; the optimiser
builds 10.8 GW less of it and replaces the energy with new wind (+54.8 TWh), existing coal (+61.6 TWh, every year from 2028, most
in 2032-34) and gas (+12.6 TWh). On c5d the same cap cut solar by 8.1 GW and added 19.1 TWh of coal, with coal 9.9 TWh lower
in 2026-30; on c5e coal is unchanged in 2026-27 and higher from 2028. Both runs build 550 MW of lithium a year in 2026-28, more
than their nulls; why c5d's early coal fell and c5e's did not is not traced. The larger solar cut on c5e (10.8 against 8.1 GW)
goes with its null's larger solar and lithium build (27.9 GW and 13.0 GW against 24.7 and 12.2).

before 2029, and NTCSA's MTSAO 2026-2030 phases closures from 2029. The pathway output records rcFrom. The page, the build LP's

rc_ bounds for 2026-28 are written as 0.

Demand (user, 18 Oct 2026, message 199 (3); build 2026-10-17g). c5f's 2026 demand is anchored on measured 2025 demand: Eskom's
RSA Contracted Demand less exports for calendar 2025 (ESK19679), scaled to 2026 by the Jan-Aug ratio (build_demand_2026.py). Contracted
demand leaves out load served by wheeled plant, and until 17e the script added back only the H1 2026 wheeled fleet. It now adds
back the wheeled wind running through the 2025 base year: Msenge Emoyeni (69 MW, from October 2024, read from the generated
capacity file) and Castle (89 MW, wheeled to Sibanye-Stillwater from about the end of March 2025; Mining Weekly, 1 Apr 2025), each
on the model's 2025 wind shape (35.5% capacity factor): 0.426 TWh into the 2025 base and the Jan-Aug ratio's 2026 side, and hour
by hour in September-December. Added a year in 2026: 0.491 TWh (Msenge 0.214, Castle 0.277; Mining Weekly put Castle at about
0.309); domestic grid demand 2026 187.67 to 188.16 TWh, the Jan-Aug ratio 0.9519 to 0.9525. Castle is not in the base, but it
is in the committed 2026 wind floor (below), so c5f supplies its load from Castle counted as new build. The 2025 backcast series (demand_2025) is unchanged: its preset runs
Eskom's own wind fleet (windMW 3,900), without wheeled plant. Until this change (17e) the caveat was that c5f supplied Msenge's
output against demand without its load.

35.5% capacity factor, as for every wheeled plant in the add-back); RESULTS 'the 2025 demand step' uses 0.31 TWh, Mining Weekly's
'about 309 GWh a year' (1 Apr 2025), the owner's expected yield at about 39.6%; the published figure is the better estimate of

### Planning reserve margin in the build LP: 10% over peak on firm capacity, no source; wind and solar get no credit, storage min(power, energy / 4 h); it binds in c5c in every year 2030-40 and sets c5c's firm capacity; the stress margin, the stress-target rows and the reserve slack do not bind (user, 16 Oct 2026, messages 129 (2) and 131 (2))

What it is (index.html, bldBuildLP, row res_<year>; in the code since it entered this repository, 1 Oct 2026). Each year:
credited storage + new CCGT + new open-cycle (LNG and diesel) - EAF x early-retired coal >= 1.10 x peak - firm, where peak is
the highest hourly demand on the year's represented days (stress windows left out) and firm is standing coal at its mean
availability (EAF), nuclear, hydro and imports at their availability factors, existing pumped storage, existing diesel and existing
batteries. Wind and solar, new or existing, count zero. Every store (lithium, vanadium, iron-air, pumped hydro) is credited at the
lesser of its power and its energy over 4 hours (rows ccpow_, ccnrg_, cc<tech>_). Value: 10%. Source: none recorded; it is a
modelling choice, not South Africa's criterion (that is being sourced, message 131 (3)).

Which constraints bind in c5c (its pass-1 solve, cache key 9c2e2e1eaa, objective 1,447,614,593,962.7, identical to the run's):
- res_ binds in every year 2030-2040 (shadow price R3.74m per MW of requirement in 2030, falling to R0.25m in 2040, present
  value at 8%), slack in 2026-29. Credited lithium equals the whole lithium build from 2030 (2030: 6,666 MW; 2040: 20,679 MW),
  so the margin, not energy, sets how much firm capacity c5c holds.
- Stress margin: 0 MW (no windows added; adequate on pass 1). Stress-target rows tgt_: none binding; expected shed in the LP
  0-0.35 GWh against targets of 2.1-3.1 GWh, slack 0, so no penalty. Reserve slack rsl_: zero in every hour.
- Hourly operating reserve (resv_, ASTR): binding in 37 of 6,840 hours, small shadow prices (sum R0.08m).
- Minimum builds bind: wind 2026-27, solar 2026-28 and lithium 2026-27 sit exactly on the committed-project floors (MIN_BUILD,
  LI_MIN). Those are committed projects, not adequacy rules.

With the margin off, every year still meets the model's standard; the closest is 2031 at 1.13 against 2.25 GWh (50%). The margin
buys firm lithium and open-cycle plant that the engine's adequacy test does not need; without it the optimiser builds more wind and
CCGT and less solar and lithium. Caveat: the standard is the model's own (half of 0.002% of demand); NTCSA's medium-term test is
20 GWh a year (below), so every run here is far inside it.

South Africa's criteria (message 131 (3), research helper, 16 Oct 2026; SOURCES 'Adequacy criteria'): IRP 2025 states no numeric
criterion, only that adequacy is "measured by the volume of unserved energy, the operation of peaking generators and the
availability of contingency generator(s)"; NTCSA's Medium-Term System Adequacy Outlook 2025-2029 (30 Oct 2024) deems adequacy met
when unserved energy is below 20 GWh a year and open-cycle gas turbines run below a 6% capacity factor. No planning reserve margin
was found in either. Both read from search extracts and one secondary article; page numbers not seen.

### Build 2026-10-15f: suite and every check that changed status (message 126 (1), 128 (2)); pumped storage counted once in reserve; retail capital follows the cost cases

Suite (ESK19679.csv present), before: build 2026-10-15d (claude/comply) 815/821 (node 728/734, audit 87/87), eng5 6/6. After, on
15f as run: 814/821 (node 727/734, audit 87/87), eng5 6/6; after the two re-pins below, 816/821 (node 729/734). Changed checks:
- validate_benchmarks psTWh, fail to pass: pumped-storage output on the 2025 trace 3.3 -> 3.6 TWh (Eskom 4.49 TWh, band +/-25%).
  Cause: the charging rule (laGasCharge). Measured: 15d with only the pump-rating cap gives 3.3, as 15d.
- validate_benchmarks peakerSeasonRatio, still failing: 1.8 -> 1.7x (band 2.15-8.6x); same cause, no change of status.
- validate_invariants, 'unserved energy never rises as the reserve requirement rises': failed on 15e with the fuller-store order in
  every hour (0.80 / 0.35 / 0.46 GWh); passes on 15f with the order gated on forecast shedding (0.80 / 0.35 / 0.35).
- validate_consistency, new-build capital: R1.118 -> R0.965/kWh; the whole move is the wind capex (the same build with BLD_COST.wind
  at the BW6 figure gives R1.118 exactly). Anchor re-measured, tolerance unchanged.
- validate_response, drInterruptMW -> avgCost and -> loleHrs, responsive to inert: in the test's context (Today 2026, 55% EAF,
  2025 trace) the engine with the charging rule sheds nothing (0.72 GWh without it), so interruptible load has no shortfall to
  remove and its effect on cost falls to R0.03/MWh. Baseline rewritten for these two cells only.
- validate_outputs, curtailFuelCost in the coal-curtailment scenario: R16.4bn -> R15.9bn (anchor 16.7 +/- 0.7). Cause: new wind's
  correction 1.064 -> 1.00; the same build with the correction at 1.064 gives 16.4 with or without the storage fix. Anchor 15.9.
- validate_findings, two known failures, values moved: iron-air's effect on July gas 22.2% -> 13.4% (607 -> 472 GWh becomes
  770 -> 667); Fossil-free 2040 curtailment 121.8 -> 113.4 against 96.3 +/- 15%. Both from the storage fix's dispatch; still failing.

Pumped storage in reserve (messages 127 (1), 128 (1)): in _stFreeP (the storage power free for reserve after dispatch, used for
coal's reserve need in three places and the reported reserve shortfall) and reserveAvailArr, pumping units were counted twice: their
pumping load as interruptible and their full rating as generating headroom. Up to the pumping MW (2,724 MW at full pump), in every
pumping hour: in c5b_14r's 15 stress weeks pumped storage pumps in 880 of 2,535 hours (35%), on average 2,316 MW. psResOnce 1, the
default: a unit counts as its pumping load or, within the rating, as generating headroom, not both; the fleet's free power is its
rating less what it generates. ASSUMPTION (user): no credit for switching from pumping to generating within the ten-minute window.
Effect: on the 15 stress weeks none (shed and cost identical to the digit: the 14.5 GW of lithium covers the reserve in those
weeks); Today 2026 at 55% EAF, three draws: shed unchanged at 0.347 GWh, diesel +7 GWh, cost +R39m. On c5b_14r's adequacy: below,
when the check lands. Batteries keep the same form (rating less discharge plus charging load): an inverter swings from full charge
to full discharge within seconds, so that is not a double count.

Retail capital (message 127 (2)): retailComponents priced new build from BLD_COST directly, so the wind, solar and battery cases did
not reach the retail panel; it now reads bldCostEntry, as the optimiser and the engine do. Deep decarbonisation 2035: R0.965/kWh on
the central capex, R1.118 on BW6's. The pathway records the 2026 wind and solar capex it used (capex2026), and the engine check
records its own in every row and stops if they differ.

The capex is computed in the app (bldTariffCapex) from the tariff, its price base, the capacity factor, fixed O&M and life at
BLD_DISC_CENTRAL (8%), which stays at 8% when a sensitivity changes the discount rate. The earlier figures are kept as cases:
bldWindCase 'bw6', bldPvCase 'bw6' (pathway WIND_CASE=bw6 PV_CASE=bw6). The wind correction is now 'none' (default), 'farms'
(1.064) or 'bw6' (0.876, so new wind's twelve-year mean is BW6 bids' 37.24%); bldRepDaysRule 'even' restores the old days. The
pathway records windCorr, windCase, pvCase and repDaysRule, and the engine check applies the run's own; runs from before
15 Oct record none, so checking one now needs WIND_CORR=farms WIND_CASE=bw6 PV_CASE=bw6.

BW7 wind (message 125 (2)): eight onshore wind bids, 1,692 MW, of which four compliant 'eligible bidders', 932.4 MW (Green Building
Africa, 29 Jul 2025; TaiyangNews, 24 Dec 2024). Their prices were not published: the minister said 'the prices we have received are
a bit exorbitant or more than we think we can afford' (IOL Business Report, 21 Jan 2025) and gave no figures. By 15 Dec 2025 no
wind had been appointed; value-for-money negotiations continued with four solar and four wind eligible bidders, and four solar
projects (890 MW) were appointed at R532.00-532.99/MWh (DEE/IPP Office media statement, 15 Dec 2025). So the capex BW7's wind bids
imply cannot be computed; the qualitative record says they were above what the department would pay. Not found either: BW7's tariff
base date and indexation share.

BW5 recheck (message 126 (4)): the DMRE statement's per-project list gives the highest wind price as R617.70/MWh (Wolf Wind Farm,
84 MW) and the second as R601.17 (Coleskop, 140 MW); the lowest R344.25 (Dwarsrug, 124 MW). R617.70 stands; the R601.17 in an
earlier search note was the second-highest. The published weighted average R495.22 is unchanged and is what the model uses; an
MW-weighted mean of the list gives R491.60 (and R431.04 for solar against the published R428.79), so DMRE's averages are
presumably weighted by expected energy, which the statement does not say. At R491.60 the wind capex would be R17,600/kW.
Research by helpers, 15 Oct 2026; WebFetch could not reach dbsa.org, dmpr.gov.za, gov.za or engineeringnews.co.za, so four
official PDFs (one to five pages) and one news page were read with Firecrawl.

Caveats: two price bases are assumptions; the tariffs are at the bidders' cost of capital and a 20-year PPA, the model's 8% and 25
years; BW5 predates the 2022 turbine price rise. Sensitivity: BW6 capex (both cases bw6), in the run list.

### Engine storage fix (messages 125 (3) and 126, TODO 14en): spare coal and gas now charge storage ahead of a forecast shortfall, pumped storage pumps within its rating, and when shedding is forecast the fuller store gives first before diesel; on c5b_14r's 15 stress weeks the engine sheds 43.5 GWh against 123.0 and costs R0.80bn less, 9.5% above the rolling optimum against 11.4%; two weeks still shed (s01 28.0, s02 9.7 GWh) where the optimum sheds none (build 2026-10-15e)

What changed in simulate(), all under laGasCharge (1; 0 restores the earlier rule, except the pump-rating cap):
- In any hour no load is shed, when the 48-hour window's need beyond coal and gas exceeds what the stores hold, spare coal and
  then spare gas (CCGT and open-cycle LNG) charge them, short stores first, then pumped storage; never a store that discharged
  that hour. Before, spare gas charged storage only in daytime deficit hours outside the peak, never in surplus or night hours.
- Before diesel and before shedding, when the window forecasts shedding (need beyond coal, gas and diesel above what the stores
  hold), the store fuller for its size gives first; otherwise pumped storage first, as before.
- Pumped storage pumps within the rating left in the hour. A bug (message 126 (5)): where coal forced above demand or must-run
  gas had already pumped in an hour, the charging block added up to 80% of the rating again (and the old gas block the same); in
  c5b_14r's 15 stress weeks 243 hours were above the rating, 386 GWh in all. What it overstated in c5b_14r, by year, from
  c5b_14r's engine check on build 15d with and without the cap alone (cost R bn / mean shed GWh, without -> with the cap; CO2
  within 0.2 Mt): 2026-2029 unchanged; 2030 250.04 -> 250.05 / 0.41 -> 0.44; 2031 255.40 -> 255.44 / 1.14 -> 1.17; 2032 263.49 ->
  263.63 / 0.53 -> 0.61; 2033 272.86 -> 273.02 / 0.47 -> 0.61; 2034 272.58 -> 272.79 / 0.40 -> 0.49; 2035 274.54 -> 274.74 /
  0.50 -> 0.64; 2036 284.41 -> 284.64 / 1.23 -> 1.47; 2037 286.47 -> 286.70 / 1.82 -> 2.11; 2038 297.90 -> 298.05 / 1.35 -> 1.58;
  2039 306.94 -> 307.07 / 1.14 -> 1.27; 2040 317.63 -> 317.71 / 1.57 -> 1.78. Cost understated by R1.56bn over 2026-40 (yearly
  costs summed), shed by 0.03-0.29 GWh a year; every year still passes its target with the cap (2037: 2.11 against 2.58). 15d
  reproduces c5b_14r's recorded 2035 check (274.54).

24-hour rolling PyPSA optimum with every setting on (NEUTRAL=all, X_RES=1 X_MR=1 X_IL=1), unchanged: the week inputs do not
depend on the engine's dispatch. The engine figure is engineFlatILRm (eng40_cost_x.py). The weeks still shedding under 1.4 GWh
shed only in the week's last hour, where stress continues past the window and the optimum's end-of-week rule favours it. Cause of
what remains in s01 and s02: the optimum banks pumped storage over days (56 GWh in s01) while the engine, seeing 48 hours, fills it
to about 30 GWh; a longer look-ahead for pumped storage (14en (b)) is the next step if the stress margin needs it.

Reserve (message 126 (1a)): gas that charges storage raises gas output by the same MW, so the gas headroom counted as reserve
falls by what the charging load (counted as reserve, as interruptible) adds; the same MW is not counted twice. Pumped-storage
units pumping are counted both as interruptible load and at their full generating headroom (psPowerTot less discharge), a mode
switch on the same machines; that predates this fix and is listed in TODO 14ep. Neither explains the invariant failure: Today
2026 has no gas charging (CCGT output 0 in every hour inspected).

correction) for the adopted variant, which ran on the full 15e build; capex, spur and days do not enter the week dispatch.

### Coal emissions compliance switch COMPLY (build 2026-10-15d, branch claude/comply): none leaves the optimiser's LP and c5b_14r's engine check unchanged to every digit; full compliance costs R38.0bn a year from 2031 on 21.8 GW of in-scope coal (R1,746/kW-yr), Eskom's recommended plan R11.6bn (R533/kW-yr); in pass 1 of c5b_14r's null LP even the full charge retires no coal early; runs s_comply_comp and s_comply_full held (user, 15 Oct 2026, messages 119 and 122 (4))

What it is: COMPLY = none (default) / compromise / full, in the optimiser (bldBuildLP: rca_, in-scope coal retired early within the
fleet's rc_, credited the year's charge per MW), the pathway output (comply: the charge on the coal kept, by year) and the engine check
(complyBn and costComply beside cost, only when a run carries it), with a control in the build panel. Two groups (user, message 122
(4)): Medupi, Majuba, Matimba, Kendal, Lethabo and Tutuka carry the cost (Eskom's six FGD stations); every other station none (Kusile
already compliant; Matla, Duvha and Kriel close before FGD could finish). Source and settings: Eskom to the NCOP select committee,
10 June 2025 (PMG meeting 40926 and the attached presentation; SOURCES 'Coal emissions compliance cost', PR #53).

Assumptions, accepted by the user as provisional (15 Oct 2026, message 125 (4)): allocation pro rata by MW of the six (the presentation does not itemise by station);
the whole R77bn falls on the six (Kusile's part cannot be separated, so their share is overstated by it); rand year not stated, taken as
January 2025 rands x SA CPI to January 2026 (1.035); capital from 2031 as an annuity at BLD_DISC (8%) over each station's remaining life
to its last unit's scheduled closure, at most 30 years (Medupi, beyond 2050, takes 30); the charge is per MW standing, so a unit that
closes stops paying (a slight under-recovery) and early retirement avoids it pro rata (retiring part of a station is a linear
approximation). Cross-check: Medupi's pro-rata share of full compliance is R50.5bn against R41.7bn for its FGD alone (Eskom FY2026
integrated report, as reported by Business Day, 2 Sep 2026) and R56.2bn in February 2026's draft cost-benefit study. Pro rata by MW therefore puts R8.8bn (21%) more on Medupi than the
reported FGD figure; the reported figure covers FGD only, so the gap is not all over-allocation.

scenario year 2026; each of the twelve weather years 2014-2025 (capacity-weighted national wind and solar, the 2026 demand
profile). A fixed 110 GW build, not a least-cost one; prices are energy-only. Capture = output-weighted price over the
time-weighted mean price, on two bases: the engine price (marginalP, the running cost of the marginal unit, VoLL in shed

### Storage reserve decided with dispatch, the restore step, interruptible load capped and called last, and pumped storage at 3.35 TWh as a known miss (build 2026-10-14q, branch claude/reserve-rule; user, 14 Oct 2026, messages 95-100)

Rules (all in engine and optimiser alike where both apply):
- Interruptible load 1,000 MW (NREL, Demand Response at the Grid Edge, FY24: Eskom's certified instantaneous demand response
  1,014 MW), with its annual energy capped (cap withdrawn in 14r, message 101) at 177 GWh, Eskom's 2025 use of ILS and IOS (Eskom data, aggregate): a calibration to
  observed use, not a sourced contract limit. Called after open-cycle plant and before shedding (message 100; the ASTR sets no
  order, p.10). Superseded: 1,200 MW unsourced and uncapped, called before diesel (message 86).
- Storage reserve (message 97): decided together with dispatch, not set aside first. Each hour pumped storage and batteries hold
  at most their unused output plus any pumping or charging load that could be dropped, and at most their stored energy over the
  product's sustain time: instantaneous 10 minutes (ASTR p.6); regulating 60 minutes and ten-minute 30 minutes, borrowed from
  CAISO's continuous-energy rules (Non-Generator Resources, revised draft final proposal, 10 February 2010; citation supplied by the
  user), cited assumptions. Superseded: ten-minute 3 hours (message 86).
- Restore step (messages 96 and 100): with load served but operating reserve short, open-cycle diesel restores it first, then
  interruptible load once open-cycle is exhausted; each megawatt lets coal back down one, reopening coal headroom.
- Checks: 'reserve shortfall rises with the reserve requirement' and 'unserved energy never rises as the reserve requirement
  rises' replace 'unserved energy rises with the reserve requirement' (message 96), because since message 92 a larger requirement
  is met by emergency reserve and shows as shortfall, not as customers cut. validate_solve's agreement check now covers pumped
  storage's reserve too.

### Avon and Dedisa as must-run to contract end (build 2026-10-14p, branch claude/reserve-rule): on January-August 2026 levels (user, message 93), 682 GWh in c5b's 2026 January-August against Eskom's 715; two bugs found and fixed before any rerun; +R5.0bn and -0.14 Mt in 2026; provisional until the c5b rerun (user, 14 Oct 2026, messages 88, 93, 94)

Rule. Both IPP peakers run on their contracts, not on merit: a daytime level (hours beginning 05-16) and an evening-peak level
(17-20) by month, nights zero, until each contract ends (Dedisa end-2030; Avon, two-thirds of the pair, to 20 July 2031); then they
are ordinary peakers. Fuel and CO2 at the diesel fleet's rates. The rest of their capacity stays in dispatch and emergency reserve,
and while running they hold online headroom (reserve rule). What a surplus hour, or coal backed down to its floor, cannot absorb is
not run and is recorded as unmet. Must-run output never sets the price. The optimiser carries the same levels as a lower bound on
diesel output in each representative hour. Setting avonDedisaMustRun (0 turns it off). Checked: no effect on 2032 or 2035 (every
output identical on and off); 2030 carries the full 899 GWh, 2031 Avon's share to 20 July (372 GWh).

### Reserve rule fix (build 2026-10-14n, branch claude/reserve-rule): coal's reserve share was held twice and never released before shedding; both moved findings return; engine and optimiser now count the same online headroom; provisional until the c5b rerun (user, 14 Oct 2026, messages 89, 90 and 92)

without 20 GW of iron-air, default profiles; Today 2026, default profiles. reserveRule 'astr' at every default.

Cause of the stalled-year shed (0.0 to 83.0 GWh on build 14m). Three faults in the engine's first ASTR implementation, none from
the post-2030 growth term (off, or with the 2030 reference set to the scenario's own fleet, the shed stayed at 83.0 GWh to the
kilowatt-hour):
- coal's share of the reserve was withheld before dispatch and again in dispatch;
- the energy storage could serve in an hour was capped at coal's headroom, so storage energy not needed for reserve waited behind
  gas, interruptible load and diesel (CCGT 0.04 to 8.0 TWh, coal 48.9 to 43.2 TWh in the stalled year);
- the coal headroom held for reserve was never released before customers were cut (message 92, candidate (b)).

| Fossil-free 2040, weather 2016 | Rule before 14 Oct | ASTR, build 14m | ASTR, build 14n |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shed, GWh | 0.0 | 83.0 | 0.0 |
| Coal, TWh | 48.9 | 43.2 | 48.9 |
| CCGT, TWh | 0.04 | 7.98 | 0.04 |
| Seriti Green July gas without and with iron-air, GWh | 1,639 / 1,635 | 3,200 / 3,200 | 1,635 / 1,630 |

Build 14n holds the reserve once, in dispatch: coal and storage may serve load up to coal's headroom less coal's share of the
reserve plus the storage power left after storage's own share. Emergency reserve (interruptible load, then diesel) is called
next, then the storage energy and coal headroom held for reserve, and only then are customers cut. 'Unserved energy' keeps the
meaning it had for c5 and c5b. What the hour's eligible providers leave uncovered is recorded apart from it, as reserve shortfall
(reserveShortMWh, reserveShortH): Today 2026 22.0 GWh in 37 hours with no unserved energy.

Eligibility (message 90). The ASTR allows generating capacity for instantaneous and regulating reserve, so the spare headroom of
any online plant counts: coal, hydro, and CCGT, open-cycle and diesel turbines while running. A running group of output g holds
at most g x (1 - m) / m above its units' minimum stable level m, and at most its capacity less g; idle open-cycle plant stays
emergency reserve. m = 0.5 for every gas and diesel turbine (reserveGasMinStableFrac). Source: SONI, CCGT Minimum Function
Specification, continuous stable operation at 50% of module MCR, 35% for its gas turbines in open cycle; read from a search
excerpt, the document itself could not be opened from here; the author's assumption, not a South African figure. When a running
turbine's headroom covers reserve, coal held for reserve takes over that much of its output.

Optimiser. The national build LP used to credit all new gas capacity, running or not, as reserve headroom; the engine credited
none. Both now use the rule above (LP rows rgo_ and rd_; hydro headroom covers any product in both). New check in
validate_solve: the LP to 2028 is solved and every representative hour's credited headroom is tested against the engine's
function on the LP's own dispatch: 0 of 1,440 hours over (gas running in 16, diesel in 11). The regional LP (Where To Build)
still holds a flat 2,200 MW; TODO 14eh.

What changed in simulate(), each measured on the cross-check weeks before it was kept:
- Commitment (14dq): the pre-pass commits coal for net load less what the short stores and pumped storage can give from the
  surplus run before it (water-filled, at 90% of their energy, power and round trip). A run with no surplus before it is not
  shaved, so 2026 commits as before.
- Surplus hours: once the surplus is taken, coal tops the short stores up towards the window's need beyond coal.
- Pumped storage joins the look-ahead. It used to give first in every expensive hour and next after coal otherwise, with lithium
  held back; the optimum ran lithium daily and kept pumped storage back. Now, ahead of coal: pumped storage gives what the
  window's surplus would spill, the short stores what the surplus will put back, and in the day's expensive hours pumped storage
  what it holds above the window's need beyond coal. After coal: the short stores, then pumped storage, above their holds.
  Before diesel and before shed, pumped storage gives first. Its coal and gas charging targets net the coming refill.
- Look-ahead 24 to 48 hours (storageLookaheadH): the rolling optimum sees 24-48 hours ahead.

### Known limitation: the engine's look-aheads read the actual future, not a forecast (perfect foresight over 12-48 hours); build 2026-10-14r (user, message 91, 14 Oct 2026)

Checked in index.html (simulate), build 14r. Every look-ahead in the dispatch engine reads the run's own future demand, wind
and solar, the same hours it will then be dispatched against, so the engine plans with perfect foresight of net load over
each window. Coal outages are not foreseen in the storage forecasts: coal available in a future hour is the commitment plan
capped by the current hour's outage state, held forward (_fcCoal, persistence). Windows:
- storage look-ahead (storageLookaheadH 48, engine fix (B)): the short stores' energy target (_laReq) is built from netLoadPre
  (actual demand less actual wind and solar) for the next 48 hours, against that coal forecast; the code comment still says
  'perfect sight of load, weather and outages', which overstates it for outages;
- pumped storage's refill estimate (_laPsRefill) and engine B's pumped-storage hold over the same 48 hours;
- storage-aware coal commitment and the 24-hour solar-aware commitment window (next day's actual net load);
- coal's ramp-aware floor over coalLookaheadH (12 hours of actual net load);
- the long stores' rule (ldesLookaheadH 168: a week of actual net load, the code's own note that past a week foresight 'does
  more work than the storage does').

Effect, direction only (not measured): a real operator works from forecasts with error, so it holds more in reserve, commits
more coal, starts peakers earlier or sheds where the engine does not. The engine therefore tends to understate operating
cost, open-cycle and diesel use, unserved energy and reserve shortfall, and to overstate how much storage can do, most in
renewable-heavy years and weeks. The PyPSA cross-check (validation/single_node, a 48-hour rolling optimum keeping 24 hours)
has the same foresight, so it cannot detect this. The optimiser's representative windows are solved with full knowledge of
each window too. Not changed. Measuring it needs forecast series with realistic error, which is what TODO 14ea's ten-day
outlook would supply (ECMWF and GFS forecasts), so this links to 14ea. Reviewer pack: limitation 19.
Re-checked 15 Oct 2026 on build 2026-10-15a (engine unchanged since 14r; user, message 115): the storage look-ahead (_laReq) still
reads netLoadPre[k], the run's own demand less its own wind and solar, for every hour k up to storageLookaheadH (48) ahead.

### Known limitation: no inertia or system-strength requirement in the build; the engine's 6 GW synchronous floor charges nothing when coal is gone (user, 14 Oct 2026, message 75; no change to c5b)

User, 14 Oct (message 75): synchronous condensers, no change to c5b; record the limitation; say whether the model has any
minimum synchronous generation rule today; add a TODO item for after the note.

The limitation: the build optimiser (bldBuildLP) has no inertia, system-strength or minimum-synchronous constraint, so a
high-renewable build pays nothing for synchronous condensers or grid-forming batteries. That flatters the renewable-heavy
results, the no-gas case (s_nogas4strict) most, since it removes the synchronous gas plant as well as coal.

In short (user, message 77 (4)): the engine enforces a 6 GW synchronous minimum; the optimiser does not.

What the model has today (engine only, index.html at build 2026-10-14l): a minimum synchronous generation floor in the dispatch
engine, SYNC_MIN_MW 6,000 MW (slider syncMinMW, on by default), described as about 15% of peak and 'consistent with Eskom's
historical operating practice', with no source recorded. Counted towards it: nuclear, hydro, imports at IMPORTS_CF (0.88, not
the run's importsCF), the grid-forming share of battery power (SYNC_GFM_SHARE 30%, at no extra cost) and synchronous
condensers (SYNC_CONDENSER_MW 0, none in service in the model). Gas plant is not counted. When the rest falls short, the
engine raises coal output to cover the gap, which costs coal fuel; when no coal is available, the shortfall is only counted
(syncUnmetH, hours the floor could not be met) and costs nothing; the engine check does not report it. Inertia pricing exists
as an off-by-default toggle (asInertiaOn) for revenue panels, not as a requirement. So in c5's later years and in the no-gas
case the floor binds less as coal retires, and a build that would need condensers or grid-forming inverters to be
operable is neither charged for them nor flagged.

Effect on results: not quantified. Direction: renewable-heavy builds and early coal retirement look cheaper than they are;
the no-gas case most. TODO 14ed (after the note).

(a) T2: only batteries count as fast-start reserve standing in for coal (open-cycle and pumped storage no longer excuse coal
from holding the reserve); 480 runs, as the check's rule required. Its 2026 cost is R5.6bn higher (R219.3bn against R213.7bn)
and its open-cycle output 1.20 TWh a year. (b) reserveOperatingMW, base 2,200 (the ASTR's), other reserve terms unchanged.

T1 (step 1's shape) Eskom's 2026 monthly coal availability (outageMonthlyAvail from ESK19679 January-August, the engine's own
months for September-December): open-cycle output up by 70% and scarcity hours by 36%, so the April trough explains part of the
gap, not most of it.

Step 2, the dispatch rule (T2). The engine lets every fast-start megawatt stand in for reserve on coal: open-cycle 3,400 MW
plus pumped storage 2,724 MW plus batteries, against a requirement of about 2.2 GW, so coal never holds reserve back and
open-cycle plant runs only when nothing else meets load. Pumped storage alone covers the requirement, so dropping only the
open-cycle plant from that sum would change almost nothing (reasoned from the rule, not run). At the other extreme, coal
holding the whole reserve (T2) overshoots: open-cycle output 8 times Eskom's own turbines, scarcity hours 3.5 times Eskom's
interruptible hours, and 2026 fails the adequacy test. Eskom's operation sits between the two; which rule fits it is not
established from these tests.

Step 3, reserve size (T3). Scarcity hours move strongly with the requirement (55, 96, 170 hours at 1.8, 2.2, 2.6 GW) and
open-cycle output weakly (5, 10, 21 GWh). A larger requirement alone does not reach Eskom's 88 GWh within a plausible range.

Step 4, interruptible load. The engine calls its 1,200 MW of interruptible load (R4,000/MWh, below diesel) only to meet an
energy shortfall: 0.1 hours in the base, 9 hours even under T2. Eskom called interruptible supply in 348 hours, 341 of them the
'other interruptible supply' product at about 65 MW on average (22.3 GWh), which reads as reserve restoration rather than
energy shortfall. The engine has no rule that calls interruptible load for reserve, so its interruptible hours cannot match
Eskom's under any of these tests; the comparison that can is scarcity hours (reserve short of requirement), which T1 and T3b
bring to 130-170 against 348.

Effect on c5b and the sensitivities: any change to the reserve rule moves 2026 adequacy and cost (T2: R5.6bn and a failing
2026), so a rule change means c5b and every sensitivity rerun. They stay provisional (message 83 (3)). Nothing changed.

### ASTR reserve rule: proposal by product (NTCSA ASTR 2026/27-2030/31) and its test on c5b's 2026; for the user's approval before any rerun (user, 14 Oct 2026, message 85)

Source: NTCSA Ancillary Services Technical Requirements for 2026/27-2030/31, Revision 1, 12 January 2026, pp. 6-12, as read by
the user (the PDF is on ntcsa.co.za, which neither the web reader nor a direct download reaches from this session; Firecrawl is
not used on long PDFs). The 2,200 MW operating reserve is three products: instantaneous 650 MW peak / 850 off-peak (within 10 s,
sustained 10 min); regulating 830 MW each way in 2026/27, rising to 1,140 by 2030/31; ten-minute 720 peak / 520 off-peak in
2026/27, falling to 410 / 210 by 2030/31 (offline quick-start such as pumped storage, and dispatchable demand). Open-cycle gas
turbines appear only under emergency reserve (1,200 MW, with interruptible load), outside the 2,200 MW.

Proposed rule (engine, reserveRule 'astr'; branch claude/reserve-rule, off by default until approved):
- Quantities: calendar year y takes financial year y/y+1; 2027-2029 interpolated linearly between the document's 2026/27 and
  2030/31 values; years after 2030/31 hold 2030/31's quantities (2,200 MW, the document's last year; no basis to extrapolate).
  The variable-generation term the engine added above 2,000 MW of wind and solar is dropped: the ASTR's regulating schedule
  carries that growth to 2030/31. From 2031 the requirement no longer grows with wind and solar, which understates it in the
  high-renewable years; an alternative is to keep a variable-generation term above 2030's level.
- Instantaneous and regulating from online headroom: coal headroom; batteries then pumped storage only up to the energy that
  sustains the product (10 minutes for instantaneous, reserveRegHours for regulating).
- Ten-minute: pumped storage with energy (reserveTenHours), then batteries, then quick-start hydro headroom (hydro capacity x
  (1 - hydroCF)); dispatchable demand none (the model has none separate from interruptible load); coal headroom for the balance.
- Open-cycle plant and interruptible load: emergency reserve only, never counted toward the 2,200 MW; called when coal and storage
  cannot both serve load and hold the operating reserve, interruptible load first (R4,000/MWh, below diesel's R6,170), then
  open-cycle plant.
- Assumptions to confirm from pp. 6-12: peak hours 06:00-22:00 every day; regulating sustained for 1 hour; ten-minute for 2 hours.
- Optimiser: its reserve row today counts headroom on coal, gas, diesel and lithium; with the rule approved it would drop diesel
  and open-cycle gas headroom and use the same product quantities, so the optimiser and engine hold the same reserve. Not built yet.

because interruptible load, called first, covers most shortfalls. 2026 stays adequate. Not yet run beyond 2026, and the
optimiser side is not built; nothing reruns until the user approves.

### The engine lets open-cycle plant and pumped storage cover the operating reserve, so coal holds none back, and it has no rule for Eskom's reserve-restoring interruptible product (recorded as a limitation under message 84; message 85 replaces that: the base rule is to be fixed by product, proposal and 2026 test in 'ASTR reserve rule' above)

The engine withholds operating reserve from coal only beyond what fast-start plant can cover, and it counts every fast-start
megawatt at full power: open-cycle 3,400 MW (Avon and Dedisa included), pumped storage 2,724 MW whatever it holds, batteries,
CCGT and open-cycle gas, against a requirement of about 2.2 GW (the ASTR's, plus a variable-generation term). So in 2026 coal
holds no reserve back and open-cycle plant runs only when nothing else meets load: c5b's 2026 engine runs open-cycle plant for
10 GWh in January-August against 88 GWh from Eskom's own turbines (Avon and Dedisa apart, limitation below), with scarcity in
96 hours against Eskom's 348 hours of interruptible supply. The engine also calls its 1,200 MW of interruptible load only to
meet an energy shortfall (0.1 hours in 2026); Eskom's 'other interruptible supply' (341 of the 348 hours, about 65 MW on
average) reads as reserve restoration, which the engine has no rule for.

Bounds (RESULTS '14eg steps 2-4', scratch tests on c5b's 2026): with coal carrying the whole reserve the engine overshoots
(715 GWh of open-cycle in January-August, 1,203 scarcity hours) and 2026 fails the adequacy test; Eskom sits between the two
rules. Direction: the base rule understates open-cycle running and its cost in the early years and flatters early-year
adequacy. Message 84's plan (a middle-rule switch and one sensitivity, s_reserve_c5b) was replaced by message 85 before any run: the
note moves past Wed 21 and the base rule is to be fixed by product. A test of the middle rule on c5b's 2026 (pumped storage
counted only up to its stored energy over one hour, open-cycle plant not counted; optimiser LP unchanged, key 458f2a9e13 with
it on or off): open-cycle 296.5 GWh in January-August, 226 hours above 500 MW, 577 scarcity hours, 2026 shed 0.142 GWh against
1.96, cost +R2.6bn; with it off, identical to c5b.

### Known limitation: Avon and Dedisa's running is not in the model; about R6.6bn a year at the model's own diesel price on 2026's pace (R9.0-9.3bn in 2024-25), the same in every scenario until their contracts end in 2030-31 (user, 14 Oct 2026, message 83; no engine change before the note)

What runs: the dispatchable IPP open-cycle plant in ESK19679 (Avon 670 MW and Dedisa 335 MW, the DoE peakers) produced
1.507 TWh in 2024 (above 1 MW in 6,406 hours), 1.460 TWh in 2025 (6,331 hours) and 0.715 TWh in January-August 2026 (4,568
of 5,832 hours; 1.074 TWh a year at that pace), about 150-190 MW through the day and 430 MW at the evening peak, in every
month whatever the coal availability (RESULTS '14eg step 1'). Aggregates only, author's analysis, Eskom data credited. The
user reads it as contract-driven; the data shows the pattern, not its cause, and no source here states the dispatch terms.

What the model does: the two plants are inside the 3,400 MW open-cycle fleet (ocgtDieselMW, Eskom's 2,380 plus 1,005), held
as fast-start reserve and dispatched only when nothing else meets load; c5b's 2026 engine runs the whole fleet for 0.014 TWh
a year. Their capacity charge is in the model (otherIppCostR, DoE peakers R2,174m a year to 2030); their energy is not.

Cost at the model's own prices (costDiesel R6,100 + vomDiesel R70 = R6,170/MWh; carbon 0.78 t/MWh at R46.0/t in 2026, R35.9/MWh):

```
2024 actual                       1.507   R9.30bn            R0.05bn  1.18     R8.34bn
2025 actual                       1.460   R9.01bn            R0.05bn  1.14     R8.08bn
2026 pace (Jan-Aug x 8760/5832)   1.074   R6.63bn            R0.04bn  0.84     R5.94bn
```

At the 2026 pace to the contract ends (Dedisa to end-2030, Avon to about July 2031, Avon's share of output assumed in
proportion to MW): PV at 8% real 2026-31 R30.4bn gross, R27.1bn net of displaced coal; R35.8bn undiscounted.

Same in every scenario: yes for the running itself, while it is set by the contracts rather than by the system: no scenario
changes the 2026-31 fleet that drives it, so the fuel, carbon and CO2 above are common to c5b and every sensitivity and cancel
in every difference between runs. The net figure would differ slightly where a scenario changes what it displaces, which in
2026-31 is coal in all of them. It does shift every run's absolute cost (about R30bn of PV) and its 2026-31 CO2 (about 0.8-1.2
Mt a year, about 5 Mt to 2031), which matters when c5b is set beside the IRP's totals or Eskom's actuals.

Contract dates: both on 15-year PPAs with Eskom, awarded by the DoE on a build, own and operate basis; Dedisa commissioned at
the end of 2015, Avon in full commercial operation on 20 July 2016 (Avon Peaking Power press release, POWER Magazine, 25 July
2016). IRP 2025 section 3.2.1.2.2 (p.13, gazette p.24) gives the contracts as expiring in 2030-31. End dates by 15 years from
each start: Dedisa about end-2030, Avon about July 2031; the exact contractual dates are not published in the sources found.

the analysis is ours, not Eskom's). Domestic demand = RSA Contracted Demand less International Exports, as in
